item.title: Update: Karpathy’s ‘AGI Is Still a Decade Away’ — Karpathy Joins Anthropic
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Andrej Karpathy joined Anthropic on May 19, 2026, seven months after his October interview with Dwarkesh Patel. He’ll be working on pre-training under team lead Nick Joseph and helping launch a new team focused on using Claude to develop Anthropic’s models. On X, he wrote that “the next few years at the frontier of LLMs will be especially formative.”

That news is the reason for this revisit. Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away — the original takeaways post on the Dwarkesh interview — now carries:

  • A top-of-page callout about the Anthropic move, with a pointer to the Future of education chapter where Karpathy describes Eureka as the place he can “a lot more uniquely add value than an incremental improvement in the frontier lab.” Read alongside the news, that chapter reads differently.
  • A full enriched transcript at the bottom — chapter outline with anchor IDs, first-mention hyperlinks, bracketed expansions, editor’s-note callouts on factually questionable claims, and a numbered References block.

Related Posts

  • Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away: the original takeaways post on the Dwarkesh interview that this update revisits in light of the Anthropic move.
  • Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again): an earlier Karpathy talk on Software 3.0 and the decade of agents, the same speaker’s prior framing.
  • Marcus vs. Brundage: A Concrete AGI Bet: a contrasting take on AGI timelines, putting money on a near-term definition where Karpathy counsels patience.
  • Chollet: How We Get to AGI: another researcher’s account of what is still missing on the path to AGI, a counterpart to Karpathy’s decade estimate.

item.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents [1] (arXiv, February 2, 2026), Haozhen Zhang et al. (Nanyang Technological University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Chicago, and Tsinghua University) reframe LLM-agent memory operations as a learnable, evolving skill bank. An RL-trained controller selects skills for the current span — a contiguous segment of the interaction trace, typically covering multiple turns, that the executor consumes as input to a single LLM call. An LLM designer then periodically rewrites the bank from hard training cases.

Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present MemSkill, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a controller that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based executor that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a designer that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents.

Methods

  • Two banks anchor the system, with three components alternating around them.
    • Skill bank — a shared, slowly evolving library of memory skills: structured templates, each with a short description, a “when to use” condition, a “how to apply” procedure, and constraints. The executor consumes a selected subset as guidance for one LLM call over a text span. It starts from four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) and grows as training proceeds.
    • Memory bank — per-trace: the running set of extracted memories the executor accumulates and rewrites for a single interaction. Updated every span.
  • The controller (a lightweight multilayer perceptron over a shared encoder) scores each skill in the current skill bank by dot-product between a state embedding and a per-skill embedding , then selects an ordered Top- set without replacement. Here is the current span, the memories retrieved from the trace’s memory bank, the natural-language description of skill in the skill bank, and , are the two heads sharing an encoder backbone.
  • The executor (a frozen LLM) applies the selected skills in one pass to update the trace’s memory bank.
  • The designer (also a frozen LLM) periodically mines a sliding hard-case buffer, clusters the failures, and proposes refinements to existing skills or new skills — edits that land in the skill bank, not the memory bank.
  • Controller training:
    • Algorithm. PPO [2] with downstream task reward (F1, success rate, etc.) as the optimization signal.
    • Top- sampling. Selecting an ordered Top- set without replacement factorizes the joint log-probability via the standard sequential rule, so PPO can score the whole subset selection.
    • Rollback on regression. Snapshots roll back if a skill-bank update degrades training reward, so a bad designer edit can’t poison the policy.
    • Exploration bias. After each evolution step, exploration is briefly biased toward newly introduced skills, giving them a fair chance at being selected before low scores filter them out.

Results

  • Setup. Four benchmarks — LoCoMo [3] and LongMemEval [4] for conversational memory, ALFWorld [5] for embodied tasks, and HotpotQA [6] for cross-distribution skill transfer. Two base LLMs: LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct. MemSkill is trained only on LLaMA; Qwen and LongMemEval results are zero-shot transfers of the learned skill bank.
  • Main comparison (Table 1 below). Across the two base-model blocks, MemSkill leads every benchmark; ▲ marks settings evaluated by pure transfer (no training on that base model or dataset), and bold marks the best score within each block.
    • LLaMA block: LLM-judge average 55.19 against the strongest baseline at 42.23 (A-MEM), with ALFWorld success rates of 47.86 / 47.01 on seen / unseen splits versus 40.71 / 38.06 for the runners-up. (LLM-judge: a separate LLM scores each predicted answer against the gold answer for semantic match — the headline metric for open-ended conversational QA, where token-level F1 misses semantic equivalence.)
    • Qwen transfer (zero-shot): ALFWorld 60.00 / 64.18 success rates without any retraining, against ~57 / 54 for CoN.
  • Component ablations (Table 2 below). On LoCoMo (LLM-judge), removing the controller drops LLaMA from 50.96 to 45.86 and Qwen from 52.07 to 41.24; removing the designer drops them to 44.11 and 34.71. The Qwen gap is bigger, suggesting the evolved skill bank carries most of the cross-model transfer benefit; the controller policy alone doesn’t transfer as well.
  • Distribution-shift transfer (Figure 3 below). The LoCoMo-trained skill bank is ported to long-document QA on HotpotQA at three concatenation budgets — no HotpotQA-specific training; the controller scores from the LoCoMo-trained bank with varied at test time. MemSkill at holds the lead at every budget, but the gap to lower widens as documents pile up — at 200 docs, scores 66.80 while drops to 58.20.

My Notes

  • Operator-level evolution. The closest learning-based siblings, Memory-R1 [7] and Mem-α [8], both RL-train memory management against downstream task signals, but with a fixed primitive set (add/update/delete/skip and friends). MemSkill’s contribution is that the skill bank itself is learnable: the four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) serve as starter templates rather than a frozen action set. The designer can refine those starting templates and add brand-new skills written from scratch as natural-language templates for failure modes the bank doesn’t yet cover. The controller adapts because skills are scored by description-embedding rather than a fixed action head. The cross-model transfer ablation supports the reading: most of the Qwen-side gain (52.07 → 34.71 without designer) comes from the evolved bank rather than the controller policy.
  • The “skill” abstraction here is not a callable. In the Anthropic Skills sense, a skill is a packaged routine the agent invokes with explicit arguments and a return value; the API/Tool/Skill ladder treats it as the layer where judgment and sequencing live. MemSkill’s “skills” don’t take per-skill arguments. They all share the same implicit context (the current span and retrieved memories), and the executor combines the selected as joint guidance for a single LLM call. They’re closer to selection priors and prompt fragments than to callable routines. The gains here come from learning over a discrete library of prompt fragments under shared context, rather than from a calling protocol.
  • LLM-as-designer is a recurring outer-loop pattern. The closed-loop alternation between (a) RL-training a learner and (b) using a frozen LLM to rewrite the design space from clustered failure cases is the same recipe as ADAS [9] for agent scaffolds and AlphaEvolve [10] for algorithms. MemSkill is the operator-level instance of that pattern. By the framework in Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning, this is still extrinsic metacognition: the loop’s structure (when to evolve, how to cluster, what counts as a hard case) is human-defined, and only the operators inside it adapt. A genuine intrinsic version would let the agent decide when its skill bank needs rewriting, instead of running on a fixed schedule.
  • “Self-evolving” overstates test-time behavior. Both the controller and the skill bank are trained offline and frozen at deployment; only the per-trace memory content updates online during interaction. The evolution described in the title refers to a training-phase alternation between controller updates and designer rewrites, rather than test-time adaptation.
  • Memory items aren’t shown directly. The paper describes the memory bank abstractly as (up to 20 retrieved per span via Contriever, so text-based) but never includes a worked example of an actual stored item. The shape has to be reverse-engineered from the skill case studies in Appendix B: dialogue skills produce short factual sentences (“who did what, where, when”), while ALFWorld skills produce structured tuples like (action, constraint) or (object, location, state). Each skill writes items in its own shape, so the bank ends up as a heterogeneous text store with no central schema. The framing of “evolving memory operations” is harder to picture concretely without seeing what those operations produce. Figure 4’s case study (below) shows evolved skills rather than the memory bank they generate.
  • Skill transfer has a budget-sensitive ceiling. HotpotQA complicates the generalization story: the LoCoMo-trained bank does port to long-document QA, but the gap between and widens sharply at 200 docs (66.80 vs 58.20). At 50 and 100 docs the two are within ~3 points, while the dialogue benchmarks were fine at . Skills evolved on dialogue traces don’t cover long-document QA well at low . At 200 docs concatenated, you need to fire a larger fraction of the bank to find enough applicable skills. The “reusable skills” claim is more conditional than it first appears: portable when the inference-time budget matches, less so under shift.

References

  1. Zhang, H., Long, Q., Bao, J., Feng, T., Zhang, W., Yue, H., and Wang, W. “MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2602.02474), February 2, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02474
  2. Schulman, J., Wolski, F., Dhariwal, P., Radford, A., and Klimov, O. “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1707.06347), July 20, 2017. https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347

item.title: TIOBE May 2026: A Statistical-Language Consolidation
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The May 2026 TIOBE Programming Community Index is out. R has matched its all-time high at #8, while MATLAB, SAS, SPSS, Wolfram/Mathematica, and Stata keep losing ground — the statistical-computing stack is consolidating around two ecosystems.

What the index reports this month:

  • R rises to #8 (from #12 a year ago, +0.31% rating change), matching its historical peak.
  • Several long-established statistical languages decline. MATLAB is near dropping out of the top 20; SAS is about to leave the top 30 for the first time; SPSS dropped out of the top 100 last month; Stata sits at #124.
  • Julia remains stuck below the top 30 despite “strong technical merits and growing academic interest.”
  • Stan is expected to debut next month, which TIOBE attributes to the rising importance of probabilistic programming and Bayesian statistics.
  • Java and C++ swap (#3 and #4) after Java 26’s release, and Zig is approaching the top 30 for the first time.

My Notes

  • Python’s drop may be a ceiling effect. TIOBE ratings are roughly zero-sum share of search, course, and vendor attention. Python sits at 19.98% this month, down from ~25% a year ago. From that height, even small simultaneous gains across many competitors mathematically pull from the leader, so the YoY drop doesn’t require a Python-specific story. An AI-assistant suppressant is also plausible (fewer “how do I do X in Python” searches per unit of code written), but it would dampen all languages, not just the leader.
  • C’s rise is harder to attribute. +1.84% YoY at #2 is consistent with the lower-level half of the AI stack (CUDA, kernels, embedded inference, where Python wrappers eventually bottom out into C), but TIOBE doesn’t break down its rating sources, so any specific driver is speculation. C# +1.19% may reflect a similar refresh from the .NET 9/10 release cycle and Unity’s continued grip on game dev.

item.title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

This is a follow-up to a 3-paper arc on self-correction in LLMs that walks through Self-Refine, Cannot-Self-Correct, and Reflexion. On Mastodon, Professor Peter Bloem (Learning & Reasoning Group, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam) asked:

NoteReader question — Peter Bloem, Mastodon

This is before reasoning models, though, isn’t it? I’d suspect that this all changed after RL training on reasoning traces came in.

Yes: all three papers in the original arc predate the reasoning-model era. None of them are evaluated on o1, DeepSeek-R1 [1] [1], or any model whose self-correcting behavior was shaped by RL on verifiable rewards. The implicit question is whether the arc’s conclusions still hold once that training signal enters the picture.

Internalizing the Evaluator

Reasoning-model training moves what used to be inference-time external scaffolding into training-time signal that the policy internalizes.

R1’s “aha moments” are emergent self-correction at inference time, with no Evaluator in the loop. The Reflexion-style Evaluator that used to gate self-correction at every inference step has been compiled into the weights. Whether R1 technically aligns with Cannot-Self-Correct’s strict definition becomes a definitional argument that misses what is actually new.

Even before R1, SCoRe showed one way to build this internalization deliberately. It trains on a two-turn structure where each attempt is rewarded against a ground-truth answer. The verifier’s correctness check is exactly the external signal Reflexion put in the loop, just moved from inference time to training time. SCoRe says “no teacher model and no oracle feedback,” but that refers to narrower things (no separate teacher LLM and no step-level oracle), and does not change the picture: the outcome reward is still external. R1 then demonstrated the same idea at a coarser grain, with the self-correction emerging within a single long reasoning trace rather than across explicit turns.

How far can it go, and is internalization the right path?

The substantive question is how far this internalization can go. Can any external verifier or evaluator that worked at inference time be moved into training-time signal that produces the same behavior at inference?

Or are there structural limits — task families where verifiable rewards cannot reach (long-form writing, open-ended dialogue, novel domains), evaluators that resist internalization because they require open-ended judgment that itself drifts? Early evidence [2][3] is that internalization works well within the verifiable-reward distribution and degrades sharply outside it, but we do not yet have a clean characterization of the boundary.

A separate question is whether internalization is the right path even where it works. Training is expensive, and pushing more verifiers into the policy carries the usual risks of catastrophic forgetting and capacity trade-offs against other tasks. Even within the regions where internalization works in principle, the practical question is what is worth pushing into the weights, and what is better kept as a domain-specific external verifier called at inference time.

I suspect domain-specific external verification stays essential even where internalization works in principle. An inference-time scaffold can be swapped, audited, or updated when the domain shifts. An internalized one cannot, short of retraining the model. That asymmetry alone argues for keeping the verifier external in any setting where the verification target itself moves.

What the original arc still teaches

Viewed through this lens, the three papers in the original arc still illuminate what is important for instilling self-correction in a model. Self-Refine showed that prompt-only intrinsic feedback does not reliably work. Cannot-Self-Correct showed why — without an external signal about correctness, the model’s confidence pushes the initial answer through into the revision and the loop drifts. Reflexion showed that gating self-correction on a reliable external signal works. Whether that gate sits at inference time, the way Reflexion put it, or at training time, the way RL on verifiable rewards puts it, the structural ingredient is the same: reliable external signal. The original arc identified the ingredient; the post-2024 work shows it can be compiled into the weights for some classes of problems and not others.

Related recent work

Several recent papers approach the internalization question from different angles. The list below is partial — pointers to other work along these lines (especially generalization audits of o1/R1-style models or post-2024 process-reward-model successors) are welcome.

  • Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners [4] [4] looks at what RL training actually internalizes — which trained behaviors let the policy self-improve. The answer is a small set: verification, backtracking, subgoal-setting, and backward chaining. It is the empirical follow-up to “what is actually in the policy” after RL.
  • How Reasoning Evolves from Post-Training Data: An Empirical Study Using Chess [5] [5] (ICML 2026) extends that question into how far internalized reasoning carries. Using chess as a clean probe outside the math/code distribution most reasoning models are trained on, it tracks which capabilities transfer from post-training data and which decay.
  • Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters [6] [6] tightens our understanding of when inference-time scaffolding is worth the compute. Revision helps when the verifier is reliable and helps less when it is not, and a small verifier-guided model can outperform a larger one without scaffolding. The same verifier-quality dependence shows up whether the scaffolding is at inference time or compiled into the weights.
  • The Stechly–Kambhampati line is the running argument for limits. On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks [2] [2] shows that GPT-4 still cannot reliably verify its own outputs even on simple planning tasks, and Chain of Thoughtlessness? [3] [3] (NeurIPS 2024) questions whether chain-of-thought reasoning generalizes outside its training distribution. Both push back on the idea that internalization is general: outside the training distribution, the policy’s self-judgment falls apart.
  • Chain-of-Thought Degrades Visual Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs [7] [7] extends that skepticism into the multimodal era. Across 17 models and 13 spatial benchmarks, CoT prompting consistently degrades visual-spatial accuracy, with shortcut-learning from textual priors that hallucinate visual details when the image is absent. Reasoning trained on text does not transfer cleanly to vision.
  • Can Large Language Models Self-Correct in Medical Question Answering? An Exploratory Study [8] [8] audits self-correction in a non-verifiable-reward domain. Self-reflective prompting on MedQA, HeadQA, and PubMedQA does not consistently improve accuracy, with effects highly dataset- and model-dependent. A direct datapoint for the boundary where internalization stops paying.
  • Self-Rewarding Language Models [9] [9] (ICML 2024) tests whether internalization can happen without any external verifier at all. The model acts as its own LLM-as-judge during DPO training, bootstrapping. Promising results on AlpacaEval, but the approach inherits the question of whether the model’s own judgment is good enough to bootstrap from in the first place.

References

  1. DeepSeek-AI, Guo, D., Yang, D., Zhang, H., et al. “DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2501.12948), January 22, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948
  2. Stechly, K., Valmeekam, K., Kambhampati, S. “On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2402.08115), February 12, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08115
  3. Stechly, K., Valmeekam, K., Kambhampati, S. “Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning.” NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2405.04776), May 8, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04776
  4. Gandhi, K., Chakravarthy, A., Singh, A., Lile, N., Goodman, N. D. “Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners, or, Four Habits of Highly Effective STaRs.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.01307), March 3, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01307
  5. Dionisopoulos, L., Majamaki, N., Ammanabrolu, P. “How Reasoning Evolves from Post-Training Data: An Empirical Study Using Chess.” ICML 2026 (also NeurIPS 2025 FoRLM Workshop Oral; arXiv:2604.05134), April 6, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05134
  6. Snell, C., Lee, J., Xu, K., Kumar, A. “Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2408.03314), August 6, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314
  7. Kancheti, S. S., Kanade, A. S., Balasubramanian, V. N., Ganu, T. “Chain-of-Thought Degrades Visual Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.16060), April 17, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16060
  8. Zhan, Z., Cui, M., Zhang, R. “Can Large Language Models Self-Correct in Medical Question Answering? An Exploratory Study.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.00261), March 31, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00261
  9. Yuan, W., Pang, R. Y., Cho, K., Li, X., Sukhbaatar, S., Xu, J., Weston, J. “Self-Rewarding Language Models.” ICML 2024 (arXiv:2401.10020), January 18, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020

Related Posts

  • Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): the concrete instance of moving the external correctness signal from inference time into training-time RL reward.

item.title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Correct Their Own Reasoning?
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Can LLMs reliably self-correct their own reasoning? 3 papers walk us through their discoveries.

Self-Refine proposes a naive intrinsic-feedback loop: a single frozen LLM acts as generator, critic, and rewriter inside a prompt-only loop. The paper reports about 20 percentage points of average lift across seven tasks, claiming that no training, RL, or external signal is needed. The gains vary widely by task — large where “good” is hard to define from a one-line critique, but very small on math reasoning, where the feedback model fails to catch subtle errors.

But Cannot-Self-Correct tests the strong claim head-on: can LLMs revise their own reasoning answers without any external signal about correctness? Across three benchmarks (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotPotQA), the answer is NO. The model’s confidence carries over from the initial answer into the revision, and the self-correction loop tends to degrade rather than improve performance. The result refutes the class of approach Self-Refine belongs to.

Then we have Reflexion that threads the needle by splitting self-correction into two LLM steps. An Evaluator detects success or failure. A Self-Reflection model diagnoses what went wrong. The Evaluator’s external signal — a hand-written heuristic, exact-match grading, or test execution — gates whether the diagnosis fires at all. The ablations found however when the signal misfires, as on MBPP Python’s high false-negative rate, Self-Reflection rewrites correct code into wrong code, which is exactly the failure mode Cannot-Self-Correct documented. So Reflexion can be read as a positive existence result for self-correction with a reliable external signal, not as a refutation to Cannot-Self-Correct.

All three papers predate the reasoning-model era. A follow-up — Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era — engages Peter Bloem’s question on whether the arc still holds for o1- and R1-style models trained with RL on verifiable rewards.

Originally posted on LinkedIn.

Related Posts

  • Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): the training-time successor to the arc, moving the external correctness signal from inference-time scaffolding into RL reward.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: a framework for why a model deciding what to learn differs from running a designer-fixed self-correction loop.
  • AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking: another reinforcement-learning route to more reliable reasoning, complementary to gating revision on an external signal.

In Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Noah Shinn et al. (Northeastern, MIT, Princeton) introduce an agent architecture that “learns” across episodes purely by writing natural-language reflections to an episodic memory, without gradient updates or weight changes.

Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly used to interact with external environments (e.g., games, compilers, APIs) as goal-driven agents. However, it remains challenging for these language agents to quickly and efficiently learn from trial-and-error as traditional reinforcement learning methods require extensive training samples and expensive model fine-tuning. We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback. Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials. Reflexion is flexible enough to incorporate various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals, and obtains significant improvements over a baseline agent across diverse tasks (sequential decision-making, coding, language reasoning). For example, Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%.

Methods

The agent operates by interaction: at each step it emits an action — a tool call, environment command, or free-form answer — and the environment returns an observation. A single attempt at the task is an episode (also called a trial), and the action-observation sequence within one episode is the trajectory () — the agent’s short-term memory.

The Reflexion framework factors the agent into three roles. The Self-Reflection model is always an LLM. The Actor is always an LLM, and in most setups the same LLM as the Self-Reflection model, with different prompts. The Evaluator can be an LLM but is often a non-LLM signal: a hand-written heuristic, exact-match grading, or the pass/fail of a generated test suite.

  • Actor () — an LLM whose weights, together with the current experience buffer, jointly parameterize the policy from which each next action is sampled ().
  • Evaluator () — scores the resulting trajectory: a hand-written heuristic (or an LLM-as-judge variant) on AlfWorld, the pass/fail of self-generated unit tests on HumanEval, exact-match grading on HotPotQA’s final answer.
  • Self-Reflection () — takes the trajectory plus the evaluator’s signal and produces a short natural-language reflection (e.g. “I failed because I assumed they both had the same professions”), appended to the experience buffer — the agent’s long-term memory that persists across episodes.

On the next episode, the Actor is conditioned on the accumulated experience and attempts the task again. The LLM weights stay fixed; the only thing that updates between episodes is the experience text. The “reinforcement signal” is literally the reflection text the Self-Reflection model writes after each failure.

Results

The paper evaluates Reflexion on three task families:

  • AlfWorld [2] [2] (sequential decision-making, 134 task instances) — Reflexion adds 22 percentage points absolute over a ReAct [3] [3] baseline within 12 iterative learning steps, and the best variant solves 130 of 134 tasks. Figure 3(a) tracks cumulative tasks solved by trial number under both self-evaluation modes (a hand-written heuristic and a GPT-as-judge classifier); 3(b) decomposes the residual failures into hallucination and inefficient planning — both decay steadily under Reflexion, while the ReAct-only baseline plateaus.
  • HotPotQA [4] [4] (multi-hop reasoning) — Reflexion improves accuracy by 20 points on a 100-question subset. Figure 4 separates the contribution: (a) Reflexion benefits both ReAct and Chain-of-Thought actors; (b) the gain holds even when the actor is given the ground-truth context, so it isn’t just better retrieval; (c) decomposes the lift between including past trajectories (episodic memory) and the verbal Self-Reflection step. Episodic memory accounts for most of the gain, and Self-Reflection adds an 8-point boost on top.
  • HumanEval [5] [5] (Python coding, GPT-4 as Actor) — Reflexion reaches 91% pass@1 versus the reported 80% GPT-4 baseline (11-point gain). Table 1 shows the gain is consistent across languages and benchmarks: HumanEval Rust 60 → 68, MBPP [6] [6] (Mostly Basic Programming Problems) Rust 71 → 75. The paper also introduces LeetcodeHardGym, a benchmark of 40 hard-rated Leetcode problems with scaffolding across 19 programming languages, but only reports results on the Python subset (7.5 → 15); the multi-language scope is released as an artifact, not used in any reported experiment. The exception to the across-the-board gains is MBPP Python, where Reflexion (77.1) underperforms the GPT-4 baseline (80.1) — see the test-generation table below.

The paper’s ablations compare self-generated unit tests vs ground-truth tests as the evaluation signal, examine memory-length effects, and separate the contribution of the Evaluator from the Self-Reflection step. Two things to flag about Table 2 before reading. First, the test suites used as the Evaluator’s signal are all LLM-generated: Reflexion’s procedure is the same on every code benchmark — the Actor writes tests from the problem description (with chain-of-thought prompting), filters for syntactic validity, and uses those tests’ pass/fail as the signal. MBPP ships with its own curated tests, but Reflexion doesn’t use them; the model generates fresh tests from the prompt. Second, the four diagnostic columns are conditional probabilities: TP and FP are conditional on tests passing (TP + FP = 1), FN and TN on tests failing (FN + TN = 1).

The Base and Reflexion columns are pass@1 — the approach’s headline accuracy with and without the Reflexion loop. The TP / FN / FP / TN columns rate the LLM-generated tests as a classifier of solution correctness, and they predict approach performance directly. HumanEval Python’s tests are clean — TP=0.99, FP=0.01 — and Reflexion lifts 0.80 → 0.91. MBPP Python’s tests are noisy on both sides: FP=0.16 lets buggy code through, FN=0.59 means most “test failures” were actually correct solutions the loop then rewrites, and Reflexion drops to 0.77.

The paper doesn’t diagnose why MBPP’s LLM-generated tests are noisier, but the prompt structure of the two benchmarks is a plausible explanation: HumanEval prompts are docstrings that often include doctest-style I/O examples (the LLM can crib from those when writing tests), while MBPP prompts are bare natural-language sentences (“Write a function to remove duplicates…”) with no I/O examples, so the LLM has to invent both inputs and expected outputs from scratch.

My Notes

  • Verbal feedback as policy state. Reflexion is the paper that established natural-language reflection as a first-class component of agent design, and the lineage is visible across 2024 agentic frameworks — from AutoGen [7] [7] to LangGraph to the critic-refiner loops in Anthropic’s computer-use agents. What’s distinctive here is keeping the reflections as long-term memory across trials rather than compressing them into the immediate context the way Self-Refine [8] does.
  • The 91% HumanEval caveat. Later reproductions found Reflexion’s gain is bottlenecked by test-generation quality rather than by the repair step itself: Olausson et al. (2024) [9] [9] studied iterative self-repair on HumanEval and APPS and argued that “self-repair is bottlenecked by the model’s ability to provide feedback on its own code” — substituting a stronger feedback model lifts the gains substantially. Reflexion’s own ablation (Table 3 on HumanEval Rust) tells the same story: removing test generation drops Reflexion from 0.68 to 0.52, while removing the self-reflection step alone barely moves the number (0.68 → 0.60). CodeT [10] [10] makes the self-generated-test mechanism explicit; Reflexion adds a reflection step on top but inherits CodeT’s dependence on test-generation quality.
  • Reflexion vs Cannot-Self-Correct. Reflexion’s headline claim — that verbal reinforcement lifts an LLM agent — runs alongside a result by Huang et al. [11] that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct. The two don’t contradict.
    • Huang et al. define intrinsic self-correction as a model revising its own answer with no external signal, and show it degrades reasoning. Reflexion always supplies an external signal via the Evaluator — a heuristic on AlfWorld, exact-match on HotPotQA, test execution on HumanEval.
    • The structural overlap is Reflexion’s Self-Reflection step. Diagnosing what went wrong over the model’s own trajectory is exactly what Huang et al. studied. The Evaluator is upstream: it gates whether Self-Reflection fires at all.
    • Table 2 backs this up with the FN column: MBPP Python’s FN is 0.59 vs HumanEval Python’s 0.40, meaning MBPP’s tests fail on already-correct solutions much more often. Reflexion then “corrects” those correct solutions and ends up below the GPT-4 baseline on MBPP Python — 80.1 (baseline) vs 77.1 (Reflexion).
    • So Reflexion is best read as a positive existence result for self-correction with reliable external signal, not a refutation of the intrinsic-failure result.
  • Memory-as-parameters has a context budget. The paper writes the policy as with — the memory is part of the parameter set. The interesting question is what learning in token space gives up. First, the experience is task-specific and doesn’t transfer: every new task starts with an empty buffer. Second, as the buffer grows across trials, the Actor’s context budget becomes the bottleneck, so the effective “learning rate” is bounded by how much context the system can spend per inference. Later work on extending effective context (MemGPT [12] [12]) and agent-specific long-context finetuning is partly a response to this limit.

item.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet [1] (ICLR 2024), Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, and Denny Zhou (Google DeepMind + UIUC) argue that intrinsic self-correction — where a model revises its own reasoning answer with no external signal about correctness — does not improve and often degrades performance on reasoning benchmarks.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a groundbreaking technology with their unparalleled text generation capabilities across various applications. Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the accuracy and appropriateness of their generated content. A contemporary methodology, self-correction, has been proposed as a remedy to these issues. Building upon this premise, this paper critically examines the role and efficacy of self-correction within LLMs, shedding light on its true potential and limitations. Central to our investigation is the notion of intrinsic self-correction, whereby an LLM attempts to correct its initial responses based solely on its inherent capabilities, without the crutch of external feedback. In the context of reasoning, our research indicates that LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction. Drawing from these insights, we offer suggestions for future research and practical applications in this field.

Methods

The paper isolates intrinsic self-correction by stripping out the external verifier that prior self-correction work relied on. In the oracle setting (used by RCI [2] and Reflexion [3] in their reported evaluations), the loop has access to the gold-label answer:

  1. Model generates an answer.
  2. Compare it to the ground truth (the oracle).
  3. If correct, stop. If wrong, prompt the model for a critique, generate a revision, return to step 2.

The oracle is doing two jobs at once: it’s a stopping condition (don’t keep revising correct answers) and a trigger for revision (only revise when wrong). In the intrinsic setting, both jobs go away. The same model produces the initial answer, then is prompted to review and revise it without any external check, and has to decide on its own whether the answer needs further work. The evaluation runs on three reasoning datasets — GSM8K [10] (grade-school math), CommonSenseQA [11] (multiple-choice commonsense), and HotpotQA [12] (multi-hop QA) — across GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo (gpt-4-1106-preview), and Llama-2-70b-chat [4]. Each round of self-correction costs two additional model calls (review, then revision), so two rounds bring the total per question to five.

The paper then re-examines two related claims from prior work:

  • Section 4 revisits multi-agent debate [5], where several LLM agents propose answers and critique each other across rounds until they converge on a consensus. The paper reproduces Du et al. [5]’s setup on GSM8K and compares it against self-consistency [6] [6] — generating multiple independent samples and majority-voting — at the same total response budget.
  • Section 5 revisits Self-Refine [7] [7] , where the same LLM generates an output, critiques it, and refines based on its own critique over multiple iterations. The paper attributes Self-Refine’s reported gains on constrained generation to a sub-optimal initial prompt that the refinement loop is largely just patching.

Results

  • Intrinsic self-correction degrades accuracy across every model tested. With oracle labels (Table 2 of the paper), self-correction improves modestly — GPT-3.5 on GSM8K rises from 75.9 to 84.3, GPT-4 on HotpotQA from 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle labels, the same prompts and models lose accuracy. After two rounds of intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5 on GSM8K drops from 75.9 to 74.7. On CommonSenseQA the drop is sharper, 75.8 to 41.8. GPT-4 holds up better but still loses 6.5 points on GSM8K (95.5 → 89.0). Llama-2-70b-chat collapses, halving from 62.0 to 36.5 on GSM8K. The cover image’s Figure 1 decomposition shows why: correct → incorrect transitions outnumber incorrect → correct ones, so the loop is on average destructive.
  • Multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched budget. With three agents over two rounds of debate, the system uses nine total responses and reaches 83.0 on GSM8K. Self-consistency with nine responses reaches 88.2 with the same model. At every matched budget, simple majority voting beats the debate protocol. The paper concludes that what looks like critique is in practice a noisier form of consensus.

My Notes

  • The RL follow-up. Two follow-ups from this same group at Google DeepMind reframe the negative result rather than overturn it. SCoRe [8] trains Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash via multi-turn RL to actually self-correct on MATH, gaining 15.6 points on top of the base model — explicitly citing this paper as the problem statement. The o1-style training paradigm builds correction into the chain-of-thought RL signal itself. The conclusion of Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet is essentially that prompting alone cannot induce self-correction in models that were not trained for it; the field has since shown that the right RL objective can.
  • The oracle-label confound is the methodological core. The paper’s most reusable contribution is naming the evaluation issue: RCI [2] [2] and Reflexion [3] [3] let the loop terminate based on whether the answer was correct, which leaks ground truth into the evaluation. Once you remove that signal, the loop runs without a stop condition and tends to drift. This generalizes: any test-time loop that uses the gold answer to decide when to halt is implicitly conditioning on it. The same issue surfaces in process reward model evaluation, where a strong external verifier provides most of the signal that gets attributed to the generator.
  • Production loops have implicit signals. Real systems usually carry external signals that the paper’s “no oracle” definition excludes: format checks, runnable code, type errors, schema violations, factual lookups against retrieval. Reflexion [3] [3] , for instance, uses an environment reward (test pass/fail, task success). The paper’s negative result is for the strict version where the model has nothing to go on but its own prior; that is the version closest to “talking to yourself,” which is also the version least likely to converge.
  • Multi-agent debate as ensembling. Section 4’s finding that multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched response budget [5][6] has been replicated repeatedly since, across the multi-agent literature, including the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failure modes [9]. Stripped of training, much of what looks like agent collaboration reduces to weighted voting on independent samples, where the sampling budget determines the result rather than the protocol.

item.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, and collaborators at CMU, Allen Institute for AI, University of Washington, NVIDIA, UC San Diego, and Google Research show that a single frozen large language model (LLM) can act as generator, critic, and rewriter in a prompt-only loop, and that this loop improves outputs across seven generation tasks without any additional training.

Like humans, large language models (LLMs) do not always generate the best output on their first try. Motivated by how humans refine their written text, we introduce Self-Refine, an approach for improving initial outputs from LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The main idea is to generate an initial output using an LLMs; then, the same LLMs provides feedback for its output and uses it to refine itself, iteratively. Self-Refine does not require any supervised training data, additional training, or reinforcement learning, and instead uses a single LLM as the generator, refiner, and feedback provider. We evaluate Self-Refine across 7 diverse tasks, ranging from dialog response generation to mathematical reasoning, using state-of-the-art (GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4) LLMs. Across all evaluated tasks, outputs generated with Self-Refine are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over those generated with the same LLM using conventional one-step generation, improving by ~20% absolute on average in task performance. Our work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 can be further improved at test time using our simple, standalone approach.

Methods

The method is deliberately minimal. Self-Refine takes an input , uses three handcrafted few-shot prompts — p_gen, p_fb, p_refine — and runs the same model three ways: produces the initial output ; emits natural-language feedback on ; and the refine step writes from the model conditioned on the input plus the full history of prior outputs and feedback (). No fine-tuning, no external reward model, no reinforcement learning. The loop halts either at a fixed iteration budget or when itself signals that no further refinement is needed. The paper evaluates on dialogue response generation, code optimization, code readability improvement, mathematical reasoning (GSM8K [5]), sentiment reversal, acronym generation, and constrained generation, with base models GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo), ChatGPT, Codex [6] (code-davinci-002), and GPT-4.

Two things distinguish the prompts from generic “what do you think?” critique prompting. First, p_fb is few-shot-exemplified to elicit feedback that is actionable (names a concrete change to make) and specific (pinpoints the exact phrase or line to change). The Figure 2(e) example — “This code is slow as it uses a for loop… A better approach is to use the formula (n(n+1))/2” — is the template: identify the offending construct, propose the replacement. Second, p_refine is also few-shot, with quadruples that show how to translate feedback into a concrete edit rather than paraphrase or hedge.

The few-shot exemplars in p_fb are themselves built from a per-task rubric — 10 qualitative aspects for Dialogue Response Generation (relevant, informative, interesting, consistent, etc.), a 5-dimension rubric for Acronym Generation (pronunciation, spelling, etc.), the missing-concept checklist for Constrained Generation. The rubric is never invoked explicitly at inference. The model learns it from the exemplars.

Results

Across the seven tasks, Self-Refine beats single-shot prompting by 5–40 points absolute, averaging around 20 points of improvement by human preference and automatic metrics. The gains are largest on tasks with multifaceted or hard-to-define objectives (dialogue, code readability, constrained generation) and smallest on math reasoning, where Table 1 shows essentially no improvement (↑0 to ↑0.2) — the paper attributes this to the feedback model’s inability to detect subtle math errors. Code optimization improves by 8.7 points absolute on GPT-4 (27.3 → 36.0), and by up to 13 points absolute when applied to Codex. Human raters prefer Self-Refine outputs at rates generally consistent with the automatic metrics. The paper releases prompts and code.

The paper also ablates the feedback prompt itself, replacing actionable+specific feedback with generic “what do you think?” feedback or no feedback at all (Table 2). The actionable+specific shape carries most of the signal, especially on tasks where “good output” is hard to define — Sentiment Reversal goes from 43.2 to 31.2 to 0 across the three feedback regimes. On Code Optimization, where “fast” is well-defined, generic feedback already gets you most of the way there.

My Notes

  • The gain doesn’t generalize beyond strong critics. The ~20-point headline held up in the paper’s own benchmarks but is sensitive to task and model. Kamoi et al. [4] [4]’s survey concludes that no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback generated by LLMs prompting themselves under fair settings, and they specifically flag Self-Refine’s evaluation as over-stating the gain (Table 4 of the survey: weak prompts on the initial-response side combined with appropriate prompts on the self-correction side). On reasoning tasks, Huang et al. [2] [2] show intrinsic self-correction can degrade accuracy on average — Table 1’s near-zero math result here was already a tell. The loop assumes the critic produces actionable feedback. When the critic is weak (smaller models make this worse rather than introduce it), the iterations don’t help.
  • Feedback quality drives more gain than iteration count. The paper omits the cleanest ablation: a single-pass critique-and-refine prompt that gives the base LLM the rubric without iteration. Without it, a substantial part of the gain on dialogue and constrained generation may be attributable to the rubric embedded in the feedback prompt rather than to iteration itself. Reflexion [3], which appeared around the same time, makes the memory question explicit: it persists verbal reflections across episodes, while Self-Refine’s history is scoped to a single input.
  • The prompt-only antecedent of o1. Self-Refine spends several times more tokens per problem than one-shot generation in exchange for task-quality gains — the same compute-for-quality tradeoff that o1-style models would later formalize with RL-trained chains, but realized through prompting alone. In 2023 the framing was novel. The test-time compute idiom only entered general usage with the o1 release in late 2024.

  3. Shinn, N., Cassano, F., Berman, E., Gopinath, A., Narasimhan, K., and Yao, S. “Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning.” NeurIPS, arXiv:2303.11366, March 20, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366
  4. Kamoi, R., Zhang, Y., Zhang, N., Han, J., and Zhang, R. “When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs.” Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, arXiv:2406.01297, December 3, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01297

  • Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): the RL successor that supplies the external correctness signal Self-Refine’s prompt-only loop lacks.

item.title: The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Anthropic published the research agenda for The Anthropic Institute (TAI) on May 7, 2026. The premise: a frontier lab can see AI’s real-world effects earlier than outside researchers can, and TAI’s job is to publish those signals so external organizations, governments, and the public can act on them. Outputs are described as inputs to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and to release decisions, with the Anthropic Fellowship as the recruitment surface. The LTBT is an independent five-trustee body that, via a special Class T share, elects a growing share of Anthropic’s board (a majority within four years); its remit was announced as long-range and extreme-event decisions, not day-to-day operations.

The agenda lays out four pillars:

  • Economic diffusion. Higher-cadence and more granular data from the Anthropic Economic Index as an “early warning signal for significant change and disruption”. Open questions:
    • adoption inequality across countries;
    • firm-level concentration of AI usage;
    • productivity growth;
    • how junior-role pipelines train senior practitioners once AI absorbs the entry-level tasks.
  • Threats and resilience. Topics feeding the Frontier Red Team and Project Glasswing backlog, framed by an explicit asymmetric tempo (capabilities advance in months, regulatory and insurance responses on years):
    • dual-use observability;
    • market-based risk pricing;
    • offense-defense balance in cyber and bio;
    • crisis-coordination infrastructure for AI scenarios.
  • AI systems in the wild.
    • group epistemology when most users consult the same few models;
    • critical-thinking degradation under increasing deference;
    • governance of autonomous agents, with naval-law analogies for unattended ships;
    • AI oversight of AI.
  • AI-driven R&D.
    • telemetry for measuring research speedup;
    • “fire drill” tabletop exercises for an intelligence-explosion scenario;
    • who governs systems that build their successors;
    • a separate “jagged frontier” question on whether models can be steered toward high-externality science (drug discovery, materials) that markets underweight.

My Notes

  • TAI is the field’s first research-agenda layer. Across the four frontier labs, OpenAI’s Our principles and its peer documents map two existing document types: declared values and deployment gates. TAI is a third type, set up to produce empirical findings the other two layers can be checked against. The Anthropic Economic Index, with more granular data and higher cadence under TAI, is one concrete commitment. OpenAI’s new “Adaptability” principle commits to updating positions as evidence accumulates; TAI is the closest the field has to an institution set up to produce that evidence.

  • Two ways TAI matters, both untested.

    • Externally, the agenda promises an “early warning signal for significant change and disruption”, language that asserts a verifiable measurement. If outsiders can’t reproduce TAI’s numbers from the published procedure, anyone acting on the early-warning claim has to take Anthropic’s word for it.
    • Internally, TAI’s findings feed into the LTBT, giving the Trust a steady research-policy stream beyond the extreme-event scope it was originally announced for. That integration becomes meaningful only when a Trust position publicly diverges from a commercial decision.

  • The R&D pillar’s telemetry could check Clark’s forecast. Jack Clark put 60% on full AI-driven R&D by end of 2028 from public benchmark trends. TAI commits to publishing the internal R&D speedup data that would let outside readers compare that forecast to actual progress. Without publication, the pillar stays purely internal and only useful to Anthropic.

Related Posts

  • OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI: the peer lab’s declared-values document this post contrasts TAI against as a third, empirical-findings layer.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: the existing data product TAI promises to run at higher cadence as its concrete economic-diffusion commitment.
  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?: Clark’s automated-AI-R&D forecast that TAI’s R&D-telemetry pillar would let outsiders check.

item.title: Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution [1], Fernando et al. at Google DeepMind propose an evolutionary prompt optimizer in which the large language model (LLM) mutates both the task prompts it evaluates and the mutation prompts that generate them, yielding a self-referential loop without any gradient updates.

Popular prompt strategies like Chain-of-Thought Prompting can dramatically improve the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various domains. However, such hand-crafted prompt-strategies are often sub-optimal. In this paper, we present Promptbreeder, a general-purpose self-referential self-improvement mechanism that evolves and adapts prompts for a given domain. Driven by an LLM, Promptbreeder mutates a population of task-prompts, and subsequently evaluates them for fitness on a training set. Crucially, the mutation of these task-prompts is governed by mutation-prompts that the LLM generates and improves throughout evolution in a self-referential way. That is, Promptbreeder is not just improving task-prompts, but it is also improving the mutation-prompts that improve these task-prompts. Promptbreeder outperforms state-of-the-art prompt strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Plan-and-Solve Prompting on commonly used arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, Promptbreeder is able to evolve intricate task-prompts for the challenging problem of hate speech classification.

Methods

Promptbreeder maintains a population of “units of evolution,” each consisting of two sequentially applied task prompts and one mutation prompt. A binary tournament genetic algorithm picks two units, scores both on a training minibatch, and replaces the loser with a mutated copy of the winner. The initial population is seeded from a library of 39 generic “thinking-style” hints (Appendix D of the paper), combined with an LLM-written problem description. The 39 hints fall into four flavors:

  • Concrete strategies — “Let’s think step by step.” (#38), “Let’s make a step by step plan and implement it with good notion and explanation.” (#39), “How can I break down this problem into smaller, more manageable parts?” (#9), “How could I devise an experiment to help solve that problem?” (#1).
  • Cognitive-style labels — “Critical Thinking: …” (#10), “Try creative thinking, generate innovative and out-of-the-box ideas…” (#11), “Use systems thinking: …” (#13), “Use Reflective Thinking: …” (#15).
  • Diagnostic questions — “What is the core issue or problem that needs to be addressed?” (#16), “What are the key assumptions underlying this problem?” (#5), “Are there any stakeholders or individuals who are directly affected by the problem?” (#21).
  • Reframings — “Given the problem specification and the current best solution, have a guess about other possible solutions.” (#34), “Let’s imagine the current best solution is totally wrong, what other ways are there to think about the problem specification?” (#35), “Ignoring the current best solution, create an entirely new solution to the problem.” (#37).

The search uses PaLM 2-L as both proposer and executor.

Nine mutation operators across five classes drive the search:

  • Direct mutation — the LLM rewrites the task prompt directly.
  • Estimation-of-distribution mutation — generate new prompts conditioned on a sample of high-fitness prompts from the population, summarizing what’s working.
  • Hyper-mutation — zero-shot and few-shot variants that use the unit’s current mutation prompt to drive the rewrite.
  • Lamarckian mutation — infer a new task prompt from correctly solved examples (the trace becomes the genotype).
  • Crossover and mutation-prompt mutation — recombine units, and separately evolve the mutation prompts themselves so the search strategy itself adapts over generations.

The four panels in Figure 2 trace the conceptual escalation: (a) direct rewriting, (b) mutation-prompt guidance, (c) hyper-mutation that evolves the mutation prompt itself, and (d) the full Promptbreeder population over thinking-styles, mutation-prompts, and the problem description. Solid arrows are inputs into the LLM in one forward pass. Dashed arrows are the cross-generational flows: each output (P′, M′) becomes the parent for the next round, and in panel (d) the mutation prompt M is sampled from the evolving population ℳ rather than being hand-written.

Results

The paper evaluates Promptbreeder on arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, AQuA-RAT, AddSub, SingleEq), commonsense reasoning (CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA), and hate-speech classification on ETHOS [2] [2]. Promptbreeder uses PaLM 2-L; older Chain-of-Thought, Plan-and-Solve, and Program-of-Thoughts baselines run on text-davinci-003, while APE [3] and OPRO [4] [4] are reimplemented under PaLM 2-L for the matched comparison. Asterisked datasets (MultiArith*, SingleEq*, AddSub*, SVAMP*) used half the examples for training and report accuracy on the held-out half; bracketed numbers in the table are quoted directly from the Plan-and-Solve paper’s text-davinci-003 results.

Headline findings (PB row leads every column of both zero-shot and few-shot categories):

  • Arithmetic reasoning — 99.7% on MultiArith*, 96.4% on SingleEq*, 90.2% on SVAMP*, 87.8% on AddSub*, 83.9% on GSM8K, 62.2% on AQuA-RAT (zero-shot).
  • Commonsense reasoning — 71.8% on StrategyQA, 80.2% on CommonsenseQA (zero-shot).
  • Beats prior prompt optimizers under matched PaLM 2-L: above APE and OPRO [4] on every dataset where both report a number.

The paper’s ablation (Figure 4) removes one self-referential operator at a time and reports the percentage change in fitness vs the full algorithm. Each ablation mode:

  • Hyper — remove mutation-prompt mutation (the “self-referential” core feature).
  • Lamarck — remove the Context-to-task-prompt mutation (Lamarckian operator: infer the task prompt from correctly solved examples).
  • SR task-prompt — remove thinking-style-guided task-prompt initialization (the seed library).
  • SR mut-prompt — remove random selection of a mutation prompt from the mutation-prompt list.

Negative cells mean removing that operator drops fitness — the operator helps. Positive cells mean removing it raises fitness — the operator is actively hurting on that dataset.

The picture is uneven. SR task-prompt (thinking-style seeding) shows the largest negative value on 6 of 8 datasets: −80% on StrategyQA, −74% on SVAMP, −73% on GSM8K, and by far the largest average drop (≈ −58%, vs ≈ −30% for Hyper and Lamarck), making it the single most important operator. SR mut-prompt is the noisiest: it’s mildly helpful on most rows but actively hurts GSM8K (+41%) and is near zero on AQUA_DEV (+1%) and MultiArith (+9%), so the random-mutation-prompt-selection mechanism isn’t carrying weight uniformly. Hyper and Lamarck are roughly comparable in magnitude, with neither consistently dominating across datasets.

My Notes

  • Self-referential framing oversold. Having the LLM mutate the prompts that mutate its task prompts hints at Schmidhuber’s self-referential weight matrix work [5] from the 1990s, but in practice the second-order mutation-prompt mutation is a further LLM call with a fixed meta-prompt. The paper’s own ablation (Figure 4) shows mutation-prompt mutation (Hyper) is roughly on par with the Lamarckian operator on average and is dwarfed by the impact of thinking-style seeding (SR task-prompt). The “self-referential” framing matters less than the title implies.
  • From operator menus to feedback signals. Promptbreeder lists nine mutation operators across five classes, and much of the win over APE [3] and Chain-of-Thought comes from this richer toolkit of edits rather than from the tournament selection itself. Since 2023, prompt-optimization research has shifted from genetic-algorithm operators toward gradient-free Bayesian surrogates (MIPROv2 [7] [7] ) and reflective critique driven by trajectory-level natural-language feedback (GEPA [6], TextGrad [8] [8] ). The field has moved toward richer feedback signals rather than richer operator menus.
  • Thinking-style seeding is the biggest contributor. The initial population is seeded by combining the problem description with a library of generic reasoning hints (“let’s think step by step,” “let’s work backwards from the answer”) listed in Appendix D. The paper treats this as a minor detail, but Figure 4 shows that removing the thinking-style seeding (SR task-prompt) has the largest negative impact on 6 of 8 datasets, with an average fitness drop roughly twice that of removing mutation-prompt mutation or the Lamarckian operator. Much of what Promptbreeder “evolves” is downstream of a good seed.

References

  1. Fernando, C., Banarse, D., Michalewski, H., Osindero, S., Rocktäschel, T. “Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.16797), September 28, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16797
  2. Mollas, I., Chrysopoulou, Z., Karlos, S., Tsoumakas, G. “ETHOS: an Online Hate Speech Detection Dataset.” Complex & Intelligent Systems, arXiv:2006.08328, June 11, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08328
  3. Zhou, Y., Muresanu, A. I., Han, Z., Paster, K., Pitis, S., Chan, H., Ba, J. “Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers.” ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2211.01910), November 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01910
  4. Yang, C., Wang, X., Lu, Y., Liu, H., Le, Q. V., Zhou, D., Chen, X. “Large Language Models as Optimizers.” ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.03409), September 7, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409
  5. Schmidhuber, J. “A ‘Self-Referential’ Weight Matrix.” ICANN 1993, 1993. Reprinted at https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/goedelmachine.html
  6. Agrawal, L. A., Tan, S., Soylu, D., Ziems, N., Khare, R., Opsahl-Ong, K., Singhvi, A., Shandilya, H., Ryan, M. J., Jiang, M., Potts, C., Sen, K., Dimakis, A. G., Stoica, I., Klein, D., Zaharia, M., Khattab, O. “GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2507.19457), July 25, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457
  7. Opsahl-Ong, K., Ryan, M. J., Purtell, J., Broman, D., Potts, C., Zaharia, M., Khattab, O. “Optimizing Instructions and Demonstrations for Multi-Stage Language Model Programs.” EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2406.11695), June 17, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11695
  8. Yuksekgonul, M., Bianchi, F., Boen, J., Liu, S., Huang, Z., Guestrin, C., Zou, J. “TextGrad: Automatic ‘Differentiation’ via Text.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2406.07496), June 11, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07496

Related Posts

  • Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE): the propose-and-select baseline Promptbreeder builds its evolutionary operators on top of and beats under matched PaLM 2-L.
  • EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers: a sibling that wires LLMs into evolutionary crossover and mutation operators, minus the self-referential mutation-prompt layer.
  • GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning: the later optimizer that replaces Promptbreeder’s operator menu with trajectory-level reflective rewrites, the shift this post argues the field made.
  • System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning: another gradient-free prompt optimizer, attacking generalization across tasks rather than per-task evolution.
  • DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines: frames the same prompt-as-parameter-to-optimize idea as a compiled pipeline instead of an evolving population.

item.title: Vibe Coding and Agentic Engineering Are Getting Closer
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Simon Willison reflects on his recent appearance on Heavybit’s High Leverage podcast and notices something uncomfortable: the line he drew between vibe coding and the responsible use of AI to write code, which he now calls agentic engineering, has started to blur in his own work. He no longer reviews every line of code Claude Code writes for him, even on production systems, and he names the trust drift directly: normalization of deviance.

What the post argues

  • Vibe coding and agentic engineering are blurring. The hard line he once drew between them, where vibe coding doesn’t look at the code and agentic engineering does, no longer holds in his own work. He’s stopped reviewing every line Claude Code writes, even on production systems.
  • The internal-team analogy. When another team hands him an image-resize service, he doesn’t read its source. He reads the docs and ships, digging in only if something breaks. He’s starting to treat coding agents the same way.
  • Normalization of deviance is the risk. Every uninspected commit that turns out fine pushes trust up, and at some point he’ll trust the agent at the wrong moment and get burned. Claude Code has no professional reputation to lose, which is what made the human-team analogy work in the first place.
  • Polished repos no longer signal quality. A polished README, a hundred commits, and full tests used to mean weeks of care. It now takes half an hour. The new signal is whether someone has actually used the thing.
  • Bottlenecks shift upstream too. Citing Anthropic design leader Jenny Wen: elaborate design processes exist because three-month build mistakes are catastrophic. If builds aren’t three months anymore, the design process can be cheaper and riskier.
  • He’s not afraid for his career. Working with agents reminds him how hard software is. The tools amplify what an experienced engineer already knows. He’d rather use a professionally managed AI-assisted product than vibe-code his own. “I can plumb my house if I watch enough YouTube videos. I would rather hire a plumber.”

My Notes

Trust accrued over a streak of clean commits doesn’t immunize the next one. In late April, a Cursor agent wiped a company’s production database and Railway backups in nine seconds and then enumerated, in writing, the safety rules it had violated. The defense against the long tail is the harness and guardrails around the agent, not more careful review: sandboxes that can’t reach production, write-fences on destructive commands, rollback paths that survive the agent’s mistakes.

Related Posts

  • Vibe Engineering: Willison’s own earlier coinage for the responsible-use end of the spectrum whose boundary this post now admits is blurring.
  • Agentic Coding Is a Trap: the counterweight, arguing the unreviewed-agent workflow Willison drifts toward trades away the judgment it depends on.
  • A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: the concrete realization of the normalization-of-deviance risk Willison names.
  • Anthropic on AI Coding: Scaffold, Not Substitute: empirical backing for treating the agent as a tool that amplifies an experienced engineer rather than replaces review.

item.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers [1] (ICLR 2023), Zhou et al. (University of Toronto, Vector Institute, University of Waterloo) propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE), a black-box search that uses one large language model (LLM) to write candidate natural-language instructions for a task, then selects the best via the zero-shot performance of a second LLM.

By conditioning on natural language instructions, large language models (LLMs) have displayed impressive capabilities as general-purpose computers. However, task performance depends significantly on the quality of the prompt used to steer the model, and most effective prompts have been handcrafted by humans. Inspired by classical program synthesis and the human approach to prompt engineering, we propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) for automatic instruction generation and selection. In our method, we treat the instruction as the “program,” optimized by searching over a pool of instruction candidates proposed by an LLM in order to maximize a chosen score function. To evaluate the quality of the selected instruction, we evaluate the zero-shot performance of another LLM following the selected instruction. Extensive experiments show that our automatically generated instructions outperform the prior LLM baseline by a large margin and achieve better or comparable performance to the instructions generated by human annotators on 24/24 Instruction Induction tasks and 17/21 curated BIG-Bench tasks. We conduct extensive qualitative and quantitative analyses to explore the performance of APE. We show that APE-engineered prompts are able to improve few-shot learning performance (by simply prepending them to standard in-context learning prompts), find better zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts, as well as steer models toward truthfulness and/or informativeness.

Methods

APE casts instruction design as a program-synthesis problem over natural-language programs. Given a small set of input-output demonstrations:

  1. Propose. A proposer LLM generates candidate instructions in one of two ways:
    • Forward generation — “here are examples, write the instruction.”
    • Reverse infilling — the proposer fills in an <INSERT> slot placed between inputs and outputs.
    Forward mode is the default and works on any pretrained LLM, but constrains the instruction to sit at the end of the prompt. Reverse mode requires a proposer with infilling capability (e.g., T5, GLM, InsertGPT, or InstructGPT’s <INSERT> token) and lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt, which the authors find more flexible. The paper uses forward mode for the Instruction Induction experiments and reverse mode for BIG-Bench. The choice is the user’s, not an algorithmic gate inside APE.
  2. Score. Each candidate is run through an executor LLM on a held-out set; the score is task accuracy or log-probability of the correct output.
  3. (Optional) resample. Monte Carlo resampling asks the proposer to generate semantically similar variants of the best candidates and re-scores them.
  4. Select. The instruction with the highest score wins.

No fine-tuning is involved and the method treats both the proposer and the executor as black boxes.

Results

The paper evaluates APE on the 24 NLP tasks from the Instruction Induction [2] benchmark [2], plus the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset and TruthfulQA [3]. It compares three sources of instructions:

  • APE — the full propose-score-select pipeline.
  • Greedy — Honovich et al.’s [2] prior algorithm, which takes the proposer’s first sample without any selection step.
  • Human — gold annotations written by the original Instruction Induction annotators.

With InstructGPT (175B) as both proposer and executor, APE reaches an interquartile mean of 0.810 across the 24 Instruction Induction tasks versus 0.749 for human-engineered prompts (Figure 1b), and achieves zero-shot accuracy at or above the human bar on all 24 of 24 individual tasks while the Greedy baseline trails on most (Figure 4). On the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset, APE matches or beats humans on 17 of 21 curated tasks. On TruthfulQA, APE-generated prompts steer the model toward truthful or informative outputs on demand, beating the human “help” prompt with 200 candidate proposals. Prepending APE prompts to few-shot in-context learning prompts also improves downstream performance on 21 of 24 tasks.

My Notes

  • A benchmark designed to favor short prompts. The 24-of-24 headline comes from Instruction Induction [2] tasks (singularize, translate, capitalize, etc.), which are short, template-shaped tasks where human prompt writers have little advantage. A crisp one-sentence instruction is close to the Bayes-optimal prompt, and LLMs can generate dozens of paraphrases of “output the plural form” cheaply. The result does not transfer to tasks where the useful prompt is paragraphs long, contains domain-specific scaffolding, or requires carefully chosen few-shot demonstrations. Later optimizers like MIPROv2 [4] [4] and GEPA [5] target that harder regime.
  • Reverse infilling, the transferable idea. Forward generation (“here are examples, write the instruction”) forces the instruction to be predicted at the end of the prompt, which is rarely where instructions naturally sit. The reverse infilling prompt, which feeds inputs on the left and outputs on the right and asks the model to fill in the instruction between them, lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt where it more naturally belongs. This matches what T5-style span corruption [6] [6] showed about bidirectional objectives years earlier, and it sits in the same family as the prompt-repetition trick for recovering bidirectional context inside a causal LM. Both are runtime workarounds for the fact that left-to-right generation can’t condition on what comes after the token being predicted.
  • Scoring dominates the compute budget. APE’s compute is spent evaluating candidates on a held-out set with the executor LLM, not generating candidates with the proposer. The Monte Carlo resampling step, the only part of APE that resembles iterative optimization, does not add much over the base proposer pool for most tasks. The subsequent line of work (MIPROv2 [4] [4] Bayesian surrogate, GEPA [5] reflective mutation, Promptbreeder [7] evolutionary operators) all attack this scoring bottleneck with different mechanisms.
  • The thin human baseline. The “human” prompts in the benchmark are typically one-sentence instructions written by a small number of annotators under Honovich et al.’s protocol [2], not prompts tuned by expert prompt engineers with access to the executor’s failure modes. The paper’s headline claim is more accurately read as “APE matches a single-shot human annotator on short template tasks.” The gap to genuine prompt-engineering expertise on open-ended tasks is a separate question the paper does not answer.

References

  1. Zhou, Y., Muresanu, A. I., Han, Z., Paster, K., Pitis, S., Chan, H., Ba, J. “Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers.” ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2211.01910), November 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01910
  2. Honovich, O., Shaham, U., Bowman, S. R., Levy, O. “Instruction Induction: From Few Examples to Natural Language Task Descriptions.” ACL 2023 (arXiv:2205.10782), May 22, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10782
