item.title: Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In the May 13 episode of Madrona’s Founded & Funded podcast, Matt McIlwain interviews Carina Hong, founder of Axiom, about her thesis that formal mathematics is the missing deterministic pillar in a GenAI stack built on probabilistic LLMs and predictive analytics. The 41-minute conversation spans her timeline of verified-AI efforts at Google, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta (each one researcher-initiated, each one wound down under commercial pressure), the result Axiom posted on the December 2025 William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition — the US undergraduate-math contest where median scores are typically 0 or 1 out of 120 — on which Axiom scored a perfect 120/120, the first AI to do so, and what Axiom has been finding as it points Axiom Prover, its Lean-based prover [1], at real hardware circuits that industry-standard formal checkers can’t handle.

With help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — Madrona’s published transcript, sliced into chapter and topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

  • 0:00:00 — Introduction: the AGI / ASI framing (YouTube)
  • 0:02:01 — Defining AGI: two competing definitions (YouTube)
  • 0:04:17 — Math Is AGI (YouTube)
  • 0:06:12 — Math data scarcity as a feature, not a bug (YouTube)
  • 0:08:13 — Formal vs. informal math — “it’s almost like a religion” (YouTube)
  • 0:13:44 — Google, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta all abandoned formal math (YouTube)
  • 0:21:20 — The Putnam story: first AI perfect score (YouTube)
  • 0:28:13 — Hardware verification as the commercial frontier (YouTube)
  • 0:31:22 — 98.93% vs. 11–12%: what the benchmark gap reveals (YouTube)
  • 0:34:22 — Math and code as the two pillars of the digital world (YouTube)
  • 0:37:00 — Team building around a shared dream of mathematical superintelligence (YouTube)
  • 0:38:03 — What autonomous proof generation looks like: the Ramanujan tau result (YouTube)

My Notes

I love this interview. Carina’s central claim that today’s GenAI rests on two pillars – probabilistic LLMs and predictive analytics – and needs a third deterministic pillar is one of the clearest articulations I’ve seen of a position I’ve held for a while: probabilistic AI has to be married to a deterministic verifier before it scales into anything safety-critical. I call it “give a backbone to LLMs.” Neurosymbolic AI is one academic framing of this idea, a research thread running since the 1980s that the LLM era has revived.

The hardware-verification discussion is particularly close to my heart: two of my early papers were on model-based diagnosis from first principles and on combining heuristic search with a formal system to address the problem [2][3]. The lesson then was that first principles are required to solve the diagnosis problem precisely, but heuristics (in this case genetic algorithms) are needed to tackle the immense search space that opens up. Today, Lean-style infrastructure can encode the problem formally, and GenAI can handle the search on top. It is exciting to see where this powerful combo will lead us to.

Transcript

What’s here is Madrona’s published transcript, reorganized for readability. The dialog stays verbatim. Three editorial layers sit on top: inline hyperlinks on first mention of salient terms; bracketed acronym expansions where the speakers don’t define them (e.g. EDA [electronic design automation]); and editor’s-note callouts flagging claims worth double-checking.

0:00:00 — Introduction: the AGI / ASI framing

Matt’s opening question: AGI, ASI, or something else?

Matt McIlwain: It’s great to be with you, Carina. To me, what’s interesting, having been an investor from day one in Axiom, is there are these debates about what is artificial general intelligence (AGI) and what is artificial super intelligence (ASI). Curious how you define, and whether you choose to define it as AGI or ASI, how you define that, and then we’ll go from there.

0:02:01 — Defining AGI: two competing definitions

The emotional definition vs. the practical definition

Carina Hong: Thanks, Matt. It’s always great to chat with you. I feel like the word AGI actually currently, it has this emotion element in it. It’s the belief that reasoning capability can be so abundant, and that you can have copies of any genius you pick in the world. And it compounds from there. You can have these geniuses work with each other, collaborate, and then ideas fuse between different scientific fields.

And then that capability then trickles down to the day-to-day life, for ordinary Joe to enjoy the same amount of capability and speed of knowledge, discovery, generation, and also applications. So that’s why I think a lot of people when they say, “We are AGI-pilled,” that’s what they mean. They believe that future is going to come.

Then there are also other people who define AGI as more practically. When that capability really flows through everyone’s consumer’s day-to-day life and enterprise workflow, because I think we’re quite ahead in the capability, and there are so many people building applications, which is great, but it’s not like a time that someone, say, in Alabama, would use whatever that is the most state-of-the-art coding model, and say UN code verification tool to build a project that is in their passion. And we’re not there yet.

0:04:17 — Math Is AGI

Matt’s provocation and Carina’s Curry–Howard answer

Matt McIlwain: Yeah. I was just in Georgia, and I think people are using the state-of-the-art of AI without realizing they’re using the state-of-the-art of AI. And of course, as you know, and we’ll talk about, the state-of-the-art is moving rapidly.

Carina Hong: That’s right.

Matt McIlwain: So you’ve made this provocative statement that math is AGI. What does that mean? And what should we take about the statement?

Carina Hong: Yeah, I think that is the DNA of Axiom. We’re very clear that, in the future, we’re going to see so many promising markets. The first one is best versus verification. In the future, we’re going to see more markets, but the DNA of the company remains math. And in our view, we think that from math and code, which, if you understand it in a sort of Curry-Howard way, are actually twins. You can then do a lot of things in the kind of use software and generation verification to control things that are in the real world, like physical engineering stuff. And then you can go to everything else. So from our worldview, math is AGI because that is the starting point of reasoning.

Note

Editor’s note. The Curry–Howard correspondence is the observation that proofs and programs are the same object seen from two sides: a proof of a theorem is a program, and the theorem is that program’s type. Lean (and other dependently-typed provers) make this literal — proofs are written as programs and checked by the type-checker. That’s why Carina calls math and code “twins”: in a Curry–Howard setting, verifying a program is identical to proving a theorem about it.

A lot of other people have different definitions of AGI. I would say that if you take the view that math is AGI, you have your action plan, you execute that a lot faster, because math is a lot cleaner. So, I was on this AI for science conference in San Francisco. It’s a really great panel, and everyone is doing experiments with the physical world. And obviously, the latency of iteration is quite long. In math, just like in coding, the digital world, your iteration time is a lot shorter.

And the other thing that’s really interesting is that because math is data-scarce compared to the other domains. So you hit some of the roadblocks a lot faster, which allows you to debug those roadblocks. So that’s, I think, one interesting difference between math and coding. With coding, we were able to make a lot of progress at the start locally, just because there’s a lot of coding data.

Matt McIlwain: There’s a ton of data, yeah.

Carina Hong: That’s right.

Matt McIlwain: Repositories everywhere.

Carina Hong: And that’s just massive amounts of data compared to, say, informal math data, or formal math data, which is even smaller.

Note

Editor’s note. The “formal vs. informal math” split is central to this interview, so it’s worth spelling out what each side means in context.

Informal math is math written in natural language: textbook proofs, research papers, chain-of-thought reasoning [4] labeled by graders, and step-by-step solutions scraped from the web. The corpus is huge and growing. It’s what general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4, o1, DeepSeek, Gemini) learn their math ability from. Correctness is judged by humans or by other LLMs — there’s no machine check that a given proof step follows from the previous one.

Formal math is math written in a machine-checkable proof language — Lean 4 [1] in Axiom’s case, but also Coq, Isabelle, and HOL. Every proof step type-checks against the underlying logic, so there’s zero ambiguity about whether a proof is correct. The tradeoff is that the corpus is tiny — mathlib (Lean’s canonical math library) has to be hand-written, and most undergraduate mathematics isn’t formalized yet. Axiom Prover, AlphaProof, and the earlier HOList [5] / GPT-f [6] lines all operate in this mode.

The “religious” divide Carina describes: formal-camp researchers think informal-math LLMs can’t scale without verification because hallucinated proofs look fluent; informal-camp researchers think formal is a niche dead-end because the corpus is too small to train anything capable. Her reconciliation — “iron sharpens iron” via Draft, Sketch, and Prove [7] — is that informal LLMs draft candidate proofs, and a formal prover fills in and verifies the steps, so better informal reasoners directly help formal ones.

0:06:12 — Math data scarcity as a feature, not a bug

Matt McIlwain: Yeah, say more about this math scarcity, data scarcity issue, because I think that that’s one of the areas that you all are creatively trying to address.

Informal math stalls above high school; Axiom’s bet on invented structured data

Carina Hong: That’s right. So, math is such a data-scarce domain. I think a lot of researchers at the beginning were kind of blindsided by the idea that, well, we just take whatever has more data in math, and take that research path, which is informal math. So what they do is they start scraping textbooks, and papers, and chain of thought reasoning data [4] through expert data labeling companies. And they try to basically build a math model that way.

It worked for a bit. So, it worked for, say, high school level, where you really just have a lot of data. And it’s a lot easier to say find human experts around the world at the high school, international math Olympia level, than say at the postdoc, or junior researcher, algebraic geometry level.

We thought a bit more first principally. We were like, “Well, we think we need structured data.” And even if that means there isn’t a lot of structured data right now, how do we invent to create structured data?

Instead of going to the unstructured route, because today we have a lot more unstructured than structured. And the structured data looks a lot like code.

I mean, it’s mostly written in the theorem-proving language called Lean, which has its own history, that’s separate from the deep learning development timeline.

And just wasn’t any Lean data. And people had to hand-code the undergraduate textbooks. They start with algebra, and then they did analysis. I remember this was 2020. I was at MIT. Fast-forward to, I think we started July last year. And we started under the belief that we can try to make progress on formal proving pretty fast. We were unclear what was the moment that formal math can catch up to informal math.

0:08:13 — Formal vs. informal math — “it’s almost like a religion”

Matt McIlwain: So take us a little bit, because there’s, I think, two interesting things here. One is this idea of formal and informal AI. Let’s unpack that.

Carina Hong: It’s almost like a religion.

Matt McIlwain: Yeah, go ahead.

“It’s almost like a religion”: why RL-for-coding researchers join the formal camp

Carina Hong: People just debate about it. And I cannot convince someone who does informal math to look at the formal math. I’m like, “You’re missing out.” Really are. And it’s usually the people who are working on reinforcement learning for other domains, like coding. They know that if you do RLVR [reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards] [8], it’s incredible, they know that math is most interesting when it’s proofs, and it’s most interesting if you assign reward for the proof instead of just a numerical answer. So, they tend to join this movement.

Matt McIlwain: Some people ask the question, “Why now? Why is this all important today?” And I usually start with, well, in a world where we’re building these LLMs [large language models], which by definition are non-deterministic, they’re predictive systems, you need some kind of system that’s a prover, that’s a verifier. How do you think about that on the why now question?

Why now: AlphaProof’s MCTS, Draft-Sketch-Prove, and iron-sharpens-iron

Carina Hong: So, first of all, we could not have been early. I think that’s right. Because we’re seeing the… I mean, informal is doing pretty well. It’s at a time when we needed to get started to play catch-up in the data-scarce domain.

I think around the time of 2024, there’s this amazing achievement of AlphaProof. And they use something called Monte Carlo Tree Search. That is quite an expensive system for a startup, expensive method for a startup to do.

It was not clear to me that was the only way. Now, in terms of why the urge to make it happen, both from my perspective and a lot of others who join us, I think it was at a time when people had more faith in structured data.

So, I think if we talk about the latter half of 2024, people thought about coding as just another enterprise application. Coding is no different from developing an AI financial analyst. It’s no different from developing an AI McKinsey consultant.

Now, obviously, we know now coding’s a lot different than that. I don’t want to talk about recursive self-improvement, but perhaps if you can agree on, at least, that is like autocatalytic. So, coding does have that advantage.

We’re not far, I think, from building an AI that can do AI research. Now, the definition of that is very loose.

You can define that as getting publications, or even spotlight papers, and ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS. You can also define that as being as good as one of those researchers out there at frontier labs.

Matt McIlwain: Yes. And some of the great researchers in academia, I was talking with our mutual friend, Carlos Guestrin, and he and some of his teams have been working on some of this area of continuous learning with reinforcement learning.

Carina Hong: Yeah. But I’m sort of fortunate and grateful that the RL coding community, they do strengthen humanity space in this other religion. And I think that’s one reason. So the code gen development. The other is the informal reasoner getting stronger, which actually also helps us. In the AI for math community, there’s this paper called “Draft, Sketch, and Prove.” [7] The idea is after you produce an informal proof, and you try to produce a Lean sketch, and you try to fill in the stories that are the voids of the Lean sketch, it works better. Now, the first part is obviously beneficial if the informal models are doing better. So, September 2024 was o1.

Matt McIlwain: And so in a sense, it’s iron sharpens iron. They’re making each other better.

Lean 4 workability and AXLE, the Axiom Lean Engine

Carina Hong: That is correct. And I think that is something that Axiom can talk about a lot and a lot, right? And we’re not talking about the only formal Monte Carlo Tree Search rigid stiff approach. I do think that we are able to get the benefits of both systems. And I think the third thing is just like after September 2023, Lean 4 becomes a lot more workable from an engineering perspective. It is still surprisingly not workable. That’s why we built AXLE, Axiom Lean Engine, which is this sort of infrastructure. There are a dozen tools, and we’re adding tools to it on a weekly basis. I believe there are people around the world, literally all across the world, using it. And people are using it interestingly with their favorite model. We see the choice of literally any model. It can be a large language model that’s off the shelf, it can be the specialized model. Even some of our competitors’ models.

Matt McIlwain: I love this.

Carina Hong: But they use all these models with the infrastructure of AXLE because it does solve a pain point that Lean is slow.

Matt McIlwain: We were together the week you launched AXLE. And it’s incredible to see the progress.

Carina Hong: Yeah. The growth curve of the user metric is quite high.

Matt McIlwain: And I think it’s at building that ecosystem out where the iron is sharpening iron that is, I think, going to help the whole community benefit. I love that framing. And I think for some of the folks in the audience that are saying, okay, how much is this getting applied, or beginning to be applied? This tension as it were between math proofs and coding. There are companies, big companies in some cases like the Amazons and Googles that are already working on this area. You’re a little bit familiar with that. Maybe talk about what they’re doing, and then maybe where you think the world’s going.

0:13:44 — Google, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta all abandoned formal math

Carina’s timeline: Google 2016 (HOL-Light), DeepMind 2021 (AlphaGeometry intern)

Carina Hong: So, I think, I certainly draw a timeline of verified AI. So 2016, Google made a pretty important bottoms-up strategic investment. There are good papers coming out of it. Playing with a language, they’re improving language called HOL [higher-order logic]. HOL List [5] is one of the papers. And then there are white papers [5][9], I think in 2019 by Christian Szegedy, a friend of mine, when he and Tony Wu, who later became xAI’s co-founder, that was like 2016, 2019. And then that’s Google, right? Mothership.

Note

Editor’s note. “HOL List” is likely a reference to HOList [5], the Google-led 2019 paper that set up an automated-theorem-proving environment over the HOL Light library, with Christian Szegedy as a co-author. “Tony Wu, who later became xAI’s co-founder” refers to Yuhuai “Tony” Wu, who joined xAI as a founding member — xAI’s public founding team lists him among the initial researchers rather than as a corporate co-founder in the CEO-equivalent sense. The Szegedy / Wu collaboration on HOList and the 2020 “Mathematical Reasoning via Self-supervised Skip-tree Training” [9] paper is what Carina’s timeline points to.

And then 2021 was DeepMind. Also bottoms up effort. One intern decides to apply this geometry. It’s just personal hobby. So, when this person was a high schooler, he has no interest in the other Math Olympiad problems compared to his interest for geometry. So he just said, “I just want to do geometry.” And that’s such a smart idea.

I sometimes think of it, because when I was a kid, I could never solve the geometry problem on the Math Olympiad in the geometric way. There’s something about my brain, and I think it’s still like now, I don’t have any sense of direction, I can’t envision spatial objects. I can’t do topology in the visual way. When I was studying geometry, I couldn’t picture those curves and surfaces. It’s almost like my brain is inhibited in that way.

On the other hand, I overcompensate by being the strongest algebraic brute force person you can find. I mean, when I was a kid, I would eat all the inequality problems.

So, from a strategic point of view, I just figured out that I can express all these lines, points, intersection points, circles, triangles, in complex coordinates, and this is a brute force method. So then I just throw away that picture. I just look at work with this complex coordinates, and I do it the algebraic way. And it would took me three times the time.

But it tells you something philosophical. That’s not quite exactly the AI corresponding thing, but it’s like, if you have a geometric figure, you can try to express it in a symbolic language, for both that human kid, and in this case, this intern of Google DeepMind, who then that was a wildly successful project [AlphaGeometry].

They expressed the geometry problem in the vector language, not Lean, even more smaller domain specific vector language. So, all these pictures suddenly become computer code.

Note

Editor’s note. The intern-driven geometry project is AlphaGeometry, led at DeepMind by Trieu H. Trinh during his internship and eventually published in Nature (January 2024) [10]. Carina says “the vector language, not Lean” — AlphaGeometry 1 used a bespoke geometry-specific domain language, not Lean; its successor AlphaProof, released in July 2024 for IMO 2024, is the one that runs in Lean.

I think they later gave up on it. I don’t really quite know. After Alphaproof, it was such a success. And so somehow the informal math team, Gemini had the mainstream voice and the non-lean approach, which is Gemini post-training, took over, they started develop evolve, that is discovery, construction not proving. So we didn’t quite hear much from them.

Matt McIlwain: Well, I think they got pulled a little bit given some of the new model companies that were making such good progress, and they had to focus for a season on the here and now, which of course creates the opportunity for Axiom Math. So, where do we go from here? Where does the field go, and then where does Axiom Math go?

Carina Hong: I still think sometimes it’s just so interesting to think about why things stopped at each of these players.

Matt McIlwain: Yeah, that’s an interesting question.

OpenAI (GPT-f, Stan Polu, Elon-left) and Meta (Llama → Mistral)

Carina Hong: And we just covered the Google story. The OpenAI story was just like, when Elon was there, with Stan Polu and other folks, they had so many papers. That was frequent within a couple months. Meaning miniF2F was the high school benchmark they established. That was later sort of really trained on, contaminated by everyone, but it was one of the initial benchmarks pointing at least a direction to go. I think there was GPT-f [6]. They tried to have early version GPT to maybe stand for mathematical functions, I think. And then they just didn’t… I mean, Elon left. They just wasn’t supported.

Facebook was doing it. Facebook was doing it. The Llama team, they spun out to be Mistral, and that was the end of story. I mean, there was Guillaume Lample, there was Fabian. You still see some of the bottoms up Meta researchers, but not really feeling like AI from X was supported. So they came to Axiom. Yeah, great opportunity.

Note

Editor’s note. The framing collapses two distinct teams. The Llama project at Meta / FAIR spun out some people, but Mistral was co-founded by Arthur Mensch (ex-DeepMind, not a Llama lead), Guillaume Lample (ex-FAIR, worked on LLaMA and earlier on formal math with Fabian Gloeckle), and Timothée Lacroix (ex-FAIR) — not the Llama team en bloc. “Fabian” is likely Fabian Gloeckle, who co-authored the formal-math work at FAIR (HyperTree Proof Search and related) with Lample; Gloeckle remained at Meta after Lample left.

But you just see kind of how short-lived each of these excellent projects are in the big places.

Matt McIlwain: I think that probably in some of these places the research had to be in service of what ultimately became the commercial pressures. And that perhaps, a few years back, the commercial opportunity to have provers that are the complementary tension to systems that are predictors, was not quite ready for prime time. But now it is.

Carina Hong: But why did they start it? So that’s kind of my…

Matt McIlwain: Well, I think they knew that it would come.

Carina Hong: I see.

Matt McIlwain: And it was maybe a timing question.

Carina Hong: Oh, they did it too early?

Commercial verification is ready now: hardware, software, blockchain

Matt McIlwain: They did it too early. That’s my theory. But now we are at this time, where people realize, especially as we go from things like chats that, okay, if it gets a little hallucinated, okay, whatever, you can go find another way to check it, check your work. But in the world of all kinds of commercial use cases, I mean, think about hardware verification, think about software verification, think about a transactional verification, or a security use case, you want some certainty that’s going to counterweight the predictability of the, as we think of them today, LLMs.

Carina Hong: It’s shocking to see how many people are using AXLE to verify things in blockchain.

Note

Editor’s note. Hong’s blockchain-users claim is not corroborated by public reporting as of May 2026. There are no case studies, named-customer references, blog posts, or social-media confirmations on Axiom’s own channels or in third-party coverage (HN, DuckDuckGo, the AXLE product page itself) that name a specific blockchain project, smart-contract codebase, or zero-knowledge system formally verified on AXLE. The claim could be based on internal telemetry from AXLE’s free playground that Axiom hasn’t yet published. There’s also a name-collision risk: an unrelated company named Axiom (axiom.xyz), a ZK-coprocessor firm that raised a $20M Series A in early 2024 — that Axiom is a different company from Carina Hong’s Axiom Math, and its presence in crypto-adjacent press may obscure whether any blockchain work is happening on AXLE specifically.

Matt McIlwain: Interesting.

Carina Hong: We’re just seeing, wow, all these interesting use cases coming in.

Matt McIlwain: And a blockchain supposedly is provable. I mean, in and of itself, the system is supposed to be provable.

Incumbents “outdid themselves”; research for impact and for its own sake

Carina Hong: I do think it’s interesting, because it’s like the benefit of being in a startup, it declares DNA, hopefully it’s doing well, it’s that you have actually that research security. You’re the core engineering group, you’re pushing on something that is on the critical path, and that critical path does not favor. We’re talking about years of good work, and at a sort of prime stage of this researcher’s career, and just compound from there. After a win, unlike in some other company, there’s a rifting company, you have finally reached that. So your point of too early is so funny. They have outdone themselves.

Matt McIlwain: They have outdone themselves, and I think-

Carina Hong: Should be forced to pivot.

Matt McIlwain: … the researchers that I have loved getting to know the most are doing research for impact. And I think at Axiom Math, you are bringing people onto the team that are excited about research for research, sake, and impact. It’s an and equation.

Carina Hong: Yeah.

0:21:20 — The Putnam story: first AI perfect score

Matt McIlwain: So tell us about the Putnam competition from last December and how this came about.

Why Putnam: > 50% of ~4,000 competitors score zero out of 120

Carina Hong: That’s right. So I think early stage startup, people get excited by a common goal. And for us, that goal, that sort of mission was Putnam. Putnam exam is very hard. So I think if people choose Putnam, that generally mean, one, they have taken that exam, which we found a lot of people whose Math Olympiad trajectory stop at the high school level, and two, they’re not totally hopeless yet. I mean, so a lot of people go to Putnam and more than 50% will get a zero out of 120.

Matt McIlwain: That’s discouraging, because these are very, very bright people, and to get a zero.

Carina Hong: Yeah, partial credit. Still, more than 50% of about 4,000 participants each year, who represent their respective universities, the Putnam teams, got zero.

Note

Editor’s note. The participant count is a rough round-up: the 2024 Putnam had 3,988 participants (the 2003 contest had 3,615). Wikipedia reports the median score is typically zero or one point out of 120, consistent with the “>50% get zero” claim. Note also that the Putnam is primarily an individual competition with a separate team component — “the Putnam teams” conflates the two.

Axiom’s perfect 120/120: first AI, alongside five human perfects in 99 years

Matt McIlwain: And so many, many people are getting zero out of 120, and there’s only been a few people that have ever gotten a perfect score.

Carina Hong: Out of, I think, 99 years of Putnam, there are five human perfect scores. We got a perfect score, and this is an AI perfect score. And this is just quite, I think, striking, even from our perspective. I personally did not do that well. I got like 39, so not even 40, and got an award for it.

Note

Editor’s note. The Putnam has run annually since 1938, so by 2025 there had been about 88 editions, not 99. The five-human-perfect-120 count is correct as of 2021 per Wikipedia; whether any additional perfects were awarded in 2022–2025 appears undocumented on public references at time of writing.

Preparing the system; the 120: top human 110, DeepSeek 103, first formal AI to beat informal

Matt McIlwain: So how did you prepare for your systems to take on the Putnam test?

Carina Hong: Surprisingly, a pretty hard part was aligning on the school, just because people were like, “Well, this is quite hard.” I mean, you probably hope to start with a high school real time tournament. But timing wise, there just weren’t any. So we started on the day of the international Math Olympia, when we had no money. So the company literally just operated that week. I mean, we had campaign chairs, foldable tables, we didn’t have a line of software written.

Matt McIlwain: Perfect startup dynamic.

Carina Hong: Yeah. So we didn’t have such a high school tournament to help climb before Putnam.

The other thing was, later we realized that this year’s Putnam, the 120 perfect score is hard for two reasons. First, top performing human of this year is 110. And the best informal LLM, sort of general off-the-shelf models is DeepSeek — 103. So this is the first time a formal AI beats an informal one in the data scar sort of disadvantage kind of starting.

Note

Editor’s note. The “DeepSeek — 103” number is cited as a comparison point but is not referenced to a publication or leaderboard; it appears to come from Axiom’s internal evaluation of an off-the-shelf DeepSeek model on Putnam 2025. Readers should treat it as Axiom’s reading rather than an independently confirmed score.

Matt McIlwain: I think related to this is this whole idea that the pace of innovation is… I’ve never seen it. And being in venture for over 25 years, the pace of change. You’ve been so deeply involved in this area for the last several years. How are you seeing the pace of development in applied AI and where it’s going, and the research?

Pace of innovation: “Ilya surge” of continual-learning pitches, the neuroscience prehistory

Carina Hong: So, I think generally progress happen for a couple reasons. Some are random, some are not. The sort of random reasons are like, somehow people start believing buy-in the religion. So I think if you think about how many companies are pitching continual learning after the Ilya circus for the podcast, you can call that like an Ilya surge.

Note

Editor’s note. Carina is referring to Ilya Sutskever’s appearance on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast on November 25, 2025 — “We’re moving from the age of scaling to the age of research” — in which Sutskever argued that pretraining gains have played out and that continual-learning and reasoning-time research are the next frontier. The Dwarkesh appearance built on the call Sutskever first made publicly at his NeurIPS 2024 Test of Time talk — “pre-training as we know it will end.” Continual learning is the ability for a model to keep absorbing new information after pretraining without forgetting what it already knew (the classic failure mode is “catastrophic forgetting”). Today’s frontier LLMs are frozen after training: post-training fine-tunes them but doesn’t let them learn from interactions in deployment. The “Ilya surge” Carina names is the wave of seed-stage startup pitches that picked up that framing in the months following the podcast.

Matt McIlwain: Yes.

Carina Hong: Continued learning, people have been pushing it since forever. Before the AI people got interested in it, the neuro AI people were quite interested in it as well, just because of a meta learning sort of in the cognitive science literature. Well, interestingly, I think they were studying why it was hard. I did my master at Oxford Neuroscience, and one of my master dissertations actually on continual learning, but from the angle of why it’s hard, from a theoretical perspective, obviously that’s not going to make things easier, better on the practical side. And there are some other not so random reasons, which is, people just realize that hallucination’s getting bad and you need a reasoning model. So I think around the time of 2022 or 2023, I looked into formal theorem proving. My main motivation has never been about hallucination. It just has never been, because I know that’s going to be a controlled problem. Just from a law of physics perspective, humanity’s not going to let this level of BS hallucination happen forever.

Note

Editor’s note. Hong’s continual-learning dissertation is unpublished — it doesn’t appear in Oxford’s research archive, on arXiv, or via Google Scholar, and her ~9 published papers are all in pure math (number theory, combinatorics, probability). Per her Rhodes Scholar bio, the MSc Neuroscience was at Hertford College, and the deep-learning work was hosted at the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit at UCL — the more likely intellectual home for “continual learning, why it’s hard, theoretically” than the cognitive-science wing of Oxford.

Matt McIlwain: Yeah. It’s almost like the benefit of having systems that can hallucinate, is that in a sense they can be creative, but the risk of a system that hallucinates is that you can’t prove it to be true.

Carina Hong: Back then it wasn’t even creative, but I think it’s like also you can choose to build contractually, kind of like controlling the downside. You can also build expensively. And I’m always the kind of people that’s in favor expanding the universe choice for both myself and others. I kind of jump around and academic disciplines, I do whatever I want. I don’t question why I’m suited to do it. And in that sense, what my interest in formal theorem proving has always been expensively. It’s like, what if we can understand the human brain? And what if we can understand the universe?

Matt McIlwain: And as you pointed out, I mean, this field, if we’ll call it artificial intelligence, actually, it’s almost the exact 70th year anniversary of that. There was a gathering at my alma mater, Dartmouth College, in the summer of 1956.

Carina Hong: Wow.

Dartmouth 1956; pre-training, post-training, continuous — “scaling is dead, but long live scaling”

Matt McIlwain: And these different pathways are now in some ways in contention with each other, but I really believe, and I think you believe, that they’re each pushing each other at a pace that we’ve never seen before. And that leads to lots of debates: reasoning systems, continuous learning, where do we get most of the benefit? There’s been a mindset of, well, pre-training was dead, that it was all over. It was all going to be in post-training, and then it was all going to be continuous. And now we’re kind of coming back around and saying, “Wait a minute, some of the newest models.”

Carina Hong: I had that line in our initial seed round pitch deck.

Matt McIlwain: I think you did. I think you did.

Carina Hong: I think something like, “Scaling is dead, but long live scaling.”

Matt McIlwain: Yes. I like that framing.

Carina Hong: I think that the point was, it wasn’t scaling instead, is that we want to scale promo data. And it was fascinating.

Matt McIlwain: And that was a year ago.

Carina Hong: Yeah.

Matt McIlwain: Right?

Carina Hong: That was so bad. That’s my point. I want to put it in today.

Matt McIlwain: Well, it’s a fun way to catch people’s attention.

Carina Hong: That’s right. It’s like clickbait.

0:28:13 — Hardware verification as the commercial frontier

Matt McIlwain: So people are curious, I’m sure, how you’re thinking about, okay, so we’re building these really interesting models, we’re succeeding at the Putnam competition. What are the commercial use cases you’re exploring? What might a verification system be able to do?

The EDA call to action; SMT-based formal checkers and the complexity-explosion handholding

Carina Hong: I think a very specific call to action is to call everyone who wants to reimagine the EDA [electronic design automation] space to just come and join us. That’s one. I would say that we have learned a lot in the hardware verification space thanks to a lot of subject matter experts, both in terms of potential customers and in terms of people who have been working in the field, and wanted to be done differently. I think that a lot of the SMT [satisfiability modulo theories]-based formal checking tools are widely used. They are widely used. But they cannot make it autonomous in a way where you need humans to do some handholding, adjusting the counter value to a smaller amount where it does not suffer from the complexity explosion. So we have learned a lot in the hardware verification space.

I think the dream really is to… I mean, if you think about verification cycles being three to four times design cycle in time, and three to four times number of people in headcount, then designing, then surely there’s something that needs to be improved.

And then a big sort of question here is, are these existing formal checking tools good enough for the more elastic demand future? And what we have found is that Lean through Improver [likely a mistranscription of Axiom Prover] could verify circuits that a formal checker could not.

Matt McIlwain: Wow, that’s a big learning.

0:31:22 — 98.93% vs. 11–12%: what the benchmark gap reveals

Hundreds of lines of Lean; Putnam overhang; Axiom Prover at 98.93% vs. DeepSeek-Prover and Goedel-Prover at 11–12%

Carina Hong: Yeah. Not an entire gigantic chip yet, I want to clarify this, but it is a small local part of the circuit. That is still too large for those formal checkers. So this is some sort of interesting margin or gain that we are observing.

And another thing I would say that’s also interesting and counterintuitive is the proof of that case is hundreds of lines of link [Lean] code. When most of our platinum problems are thousands of lines of link code, and in some of our research problems, tens of thousands of lines of link code.

So, I think it is possible that we could have not one Putnam and be able to serve this customer. So that is interesting, right? It is the sort of center capability overhang that we observe, and just across AI. But it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t win Putnam, because it’s frankly quite fun.

And I think that there could be a lot of reasons why you want to push on the math self-improving capability side, because of software verification.

So, what we have found is I think we have one of the strongest math provers in the world. And that also corroborates with we saturated the code variant benchmark, a Lean software verification benchmark. I think DeepSeek-Prover was at 11, 12%. Goedel-Prover [11]’s at 11, 12%. We are 98.93%.

Note

Editor’s note. The conversation names the gap but not the benchmark. “The code variant benchmark, a Lean software verification benchmark” most likely refers to FVAPPS [12] (Formal Verification of APPS) or a sibling Lean-based software-verification suite; the 11–12% figures for DeepSeek-Prover and Goedel-Prover are plausible out-of-the-box scores on such benchmarks but need the specific split, scoring rule, and test-contamination disclosure before the number is independently credible. The 98.93% is reported by Axiom and, at time of writing, has not been independently reproduced on a published leaderboard.

Matt McIlwain: That’s incredible. Yeah. And I think this is part of what you’re beginning to learn is that being able to build verification systems, prover systems, can be generalizable at some level. And not only generalizable, but then order magnitude better.

“Math is kind of free”: training on math transfers to domains where data is paywalled

Carina Hong: Yes. And I could argue something that’s interesting, which is, if you think about, “Hey, I just don’t have an affinity for math,” supposedly. “I just don’t care about math.” This is a very sort of extreme brainstorming exercise. And I want to train a model that can do all these things. So, I will need to collect some hardware data. I will then need to collect some software data. And all these data have commercial value attached to it, versus math is kind of free. So, if you train on math data and it transfers quite efficiently to these domains, then this is sort of generalizable, not universally, because you can’t make a good writer or poet out of it, but it’s generalizable in the best way in that you are taking a short, efficient path to tackle some of the most valuable domains where you might not have a data mode if you just pursue those domains.

0:34:22 — Math and code as the two pillars of the digital world

Matt McIlwain: I think that makes sense.

So, let’s come back a little bit then to this question of what does this mean for the definition of artificial general intelligence/artificial superintelligence? How do we put all these things we’ve been talking about in the context of math provers systems into that broader world?

The GenAI-building meme: LLMs + predictive analytics need a deterministic third pillar

Carina Hong: So, think about the word GenAI applications. And so there’s this internet meme of, they’re like a huge building, a lot of bricks, all this stuff. And then there are only two pillars, literally just two bricks here and there. And there’s all this stuff on top of it. And these two pillars, in my view right now, the infrastructure layer, are LLM and predictive analytics. Nothing else. The whole world of genAI is built on probabilistic LLM, which we don’t understand, and predictive analytics.

So it’s just from a symmetry standpoint, Matt, just from a symmetry standpoint. If you have such a stochastic system, it makes sense for you to have some deterministic component. It’s just from a symmetric. So then we want to basically be, we think of ourselves as this sort of edition, an inevitable edition in all possible futures in the AI in front layer.

Matt McIlwain: Yeah. You need determinism in a world of non-determinism.

Math-in-code, code-verified-by-math; Eric Schmidt’s “programming gives output, math gives property”

Carina Hong: Yeah. I’ll add something that is another… I like symmetry, I think it’s a beautiful concept. In group theory, you have symmetry everywhere. Another symmetry here is, isn’t it beautiful that you can express math in code, and you can verify code with math?

Matt McIlwain: I love that.

Carina Hong: I think that is just beautiful, because it’s like, in a way, there is a very clear path in front of us to unify the two pillars of the digital world. I kind of agree by so many experts. Eric Schmidt talk about it all day. Two pillars of the digital world, math and programming, math and programming. Programming gives you output; math gives you property. And output is meaningless if you don’t know what property is satisfied. My age is a number. That property, it is my age. I mean, in that sense, you have logic, and you have computation, and they’re unified, I think, in what we’re doing, and what we’re set out to do.

Note

Editor’s note. Carina is referencing a recurring Schmidt theme across his recent public speaking — that AI is replacing day-to-day programming, leaving math and formal reasoning as the durable layer underneath. Recent venues:

  • “The Future of Technology at 300” (SCSP AI+ Expo, May 13, 2026 — same day as this Madrona podcast). Includes chapters on “Why the Era of Traditional Coding is Over” and “What Should Young People Study?” where Schmidt pivots students toward foundational math.
  • Abundance360 Summit 2026 with Peter Diamandis (March 2026). Schmidt’s “20–80 human split” framing — programming output collapses to AI, reasoning and math remain the human-leverage layer.
  • Stanford ECON295/CS323 guest lecture (leaked August 2024). The earliest version of the argument that software engineering as a profession is collapsing into AI orchestration.

Carina’s specific phrasing — “programming gives you output; math gives you property” — appears to be her summary of Schmidt’s framing rather than a direct quote.

So I think that’s something that is oriented to today’s AI landscape, but there is a future. There’s a future one.

0:37:00 — Team building around a shared dream of mathematical superintelligence

Matt McIlwain: Which maybe brings me to one last question, which is, in less than a year, you’ve already built this incredible team with complementary coding, and math, and infrastructure, and a whole set of capabilities. How have you been able to do that? And what are you learning from being a founder, and company builder, and team builder?

Two theories: data-poor-plant sample efficiency; the “shared yearning for a superhuman mathematician”

Carina Hong: There are a few theories I have. One is, it could be that just formal math was so data poor. It’s like this plant is almost dead, but then you just water it, and it has beautiful flowers coming out of it. That’s one theory, right? Which means very good sample efficiency. That’s kind of the technical idea, is that if you have verified output and pairs, then grounding the natural language, have formal logic ground the natural language, you’re going to do really, really, really well.

In terms of the other sort of team building aspect, I think sometimes, and this is quite encouraging, when I was talking to folks like Francois Charton, for example, and Ken Ono, I felt like it was like there is a shared dream, and there is this shared yearning. Some people don’t state it; some people state it. That is that we all yearn for a superhuman mathematician.

And this is very interesting because if you think about in the context of job replacement, say if you have a super human AI lawyer, that means some lawyer is going to be out of job, and some lawyers might be averse to that.

Math is a field where there is a common goal that people are aligned around, and that is the pursuit of knowledge. And so it’s like, if that is a common goal, there isn’t a lot of ego around who’s going to make it happen.

And the feeling of being able to clone yourself, you’re a great mathematician, and extend yourself, and clone someone who has passed away decades and centuries ago, and talk to that, these are, I think, beautiful concepts that, somehow, because of technical reasons we have talked about, are coming into life.

And what are we seeing every day? And this is maybe why people feel motivated to work even harder. We’re seeing every day is like, we will get an email about a math problem from, say, a professor in Germany that is in Ken’s network at 10:00 AM. By 2:00 PM, four hours later, Axiom Prover generated a whole link [Lean] proof without human intervention, autonomously checked, and sent it back to that professor.

Here is a proof for your unsolved math problem. And that is daily mathematical Pokémon hunting in a funny way, but there’s something deeper, and we’re still slow to react to that fact.

Matt McIlwain: You’re learning your way through that.

Carina Hong: We’re so to react to that fact that there is hardware and software verification. I think there is endless market that is in the category of mathematical superintelligence.

Matt McIlwain: Well, that shared mission about mathematical superintelligence, the incredible team you’re building, and this ongoing curiosity to discover what the use cases are for that to impact the world, is what’s inspired us to be partners and colleagues with you.

0:38:03 — What autonomous proof generation looks like: the Ramanujan tau result

Ramanujan tau function misses 100% of the primes — autonomously proved by Axiom Prover

Carina Hong: I don’t know if the last time I saw you, I told you this news, but just their mathematical results, that after I tell people, they’re like, “I don’t really know how to technically prove it, but it sounds beautiful.” And here’s one. It’s something recently autonomously proved by Axiom Prover. So, the Ramanujan tau function is tau, and it is a function that appears frequently in Ramanujan’s lost notebook. It’s one of the fundamental functions in number theory. Axiom Prover, the AI, autonomously proved that the Ramanujan tau function misses 100% of the primes.

Note

Editor’s note. “Misses 100% of the primes” is a density statement, not a pointwise one. The open problem Carina is gesturing at is Lehmer’s 1947 conjecture that for every positive integer — verified by computation up to (Derickx) but still unproved in general. The density version, “the set of primes at which has natural density zero,” is meaningful progress toward Lehmer rather than Lehmer itself, and Carina’s conditioning on the ABC conjecture in the next turn is essential, not decorative.

Matt McIlwain: Wow.

ABC conjecture caveat; Mirzakhani, Alex Wright, and seven arXiv papers

Carina Hong: And this is assuming the ABC conjecture, of course, which is something like the Ramanujan hypothesis; a lot of people, or generalized people, just agree or assume all, but this is something that we don’t know. And so that is a beautiful result. I mean, just when we shared it, people felt like that is… I like to be this math evangelist, because I just like talking about it. Relatedly, there are mathematicians like Ramanujan in this case and Maryam Mirzakhani. They left behind bodies of work in terms of Mirzakhani, there is the dynamical systems. And recently, there is a paper that we published, in which Michigan Professor Alex Wright posed the problem. And in that case, we were able to also formalize the solution. So, verify it is correct, and actually optimize the proof and correct the proof mistakes. So, comes in different forms, some autonomous proving, some auto formalization, but we are at a point where we have, I think, seven papers on archived [arXiv] now, where the main engine is done by Axiom Prover. I think five for proving, and two for other formalizations.

Note

Editor’s note. The analogy between the ABC conjecture and the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture (“Ramanujan hypothesis”) is loose. Both are deep open problems that much of modern number theory assumes, but they are about different objects. ABC is a statement about additive relations among the prime factors of integers satisfying , while Ramanujan–Petersson bounds the size of the Fourier coefficients of modular forms. Carina’s “assumed by many, still unproved” framing is fair, but the equivalence between the two is not.

Matt McIlwain: Well, I’m excited about this idea of the beauty of math, and the applied beauty of math that Axiom, you, Carina, and your team are going to help us discover in the years ahead.

Carina Hong: Thanks, Matt.

Matt McIlwain: So thanks so much for being here with me today.

Carina Hong: It’s really great.

Matt McIlwain: I really enjoyed the conversation.

Carina Hong: Thank you.

item.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2026 Oral), Lakshya A. Agrawal (UC Berkeley), Matei Zaharia (UC Berkeley / Databricks), Omar Khattab (MIT), and 14 co-authors across UC Berkeley, Stanford, Notre Dame, BespokeLabs.ai, Databricks, and MIT argue that natural-language reflection on sampled trajectories is a richer learning signal than scalar rewards, and introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [2] while using far fewer rollouts.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted to downstream tasks via reinforcement learning (RL) methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which often require thousands of rollouts to learn new tasks. We argue that the interpretable nature of language often provides a much richer learning medium for LLMs, compared to policy gradients derived from sparse, scalar rewards. To test this, we introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that thoroughly incorporates natural language reflection to learn high-level rules from trial and error. Given any AI system containing one or more LLM prompts, GEPA samples trajectories (e.g., reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs) and reflects on them in natural language to diagnose problems, propose and test prompt updates, and combine complementary lessons from the Pareto frontier of its own attempts. As a result of GEPA’s design, it can often turn even just a few rollouts into a large quality gain. Across six tasks, GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35x fewer rollouts. GEPA also outperforms the leading prompt optimizer, MIPROv2, by over 10% (e.g., +12% accuracy on AIME-2025), and demonstrates promising results as an inference-time search strategy for code optimization. We release our code at https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa.

Methods

A compound AI system, in the paper’s (and DSPy’s) vocabulary, is a pipeline of one or more LLM-invoked modules — each a distinct prompted call (e.g., a first-hop query generator, a second-hop query generator, an answer generator in a multi-hop QA pipeline) — potentially interleaved with tool calls. Each module has its own prompt, which GEPA can optimize independently.

GEPA treats each prompt in a compound AI system as a gene and maintains a pool of candidate programs. At each iteration (Figure 3), GEPA proposes a new candidate using one of two genetic operators — a single-parent mutation or a two-parent crossover — and evaluates it on a minibatch. If the minibatch score improves over the parent, the candidate is promoted to evaluation on the full training set and added to the pool. The default operator is reflective mutation; crossover (Merge) fires opportunistically when the pool contains two candidates that share a common ancestor, have optimized disjoint sets of prompts, are both Pareto-optimal, and both beat the ancestor in aggregate — with a hard cap of five merges per run.

The two operators are:

  • Reflective Prompt Mutation samples trajectories from one candidate — reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs — and feeds them to a reflector LM that writes a natural-language diagnosis of what went wrong and proposes an edited prompt for a single module. Figure 5 traces this on PUPA [3] — a benchmark for privacy-conscious delegation, where a trusted local model must answer user queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) using an untrusted API model as a helper, without leaking PII. Starting from a short base instruction (“Create a privacy-preserving request for a powerful external LLM that can assist without learning private information about the user.”), each successful child adds a concrete nuance the reflector extracted from a failure — expanded privacy strategies, explicit PII categories and generalizations, structured output and domain best-practices, then a detailed transformation rationale, ending at a strict exhaustive protocol that bans partial redaction and demands auditable zero-leakage. The prompt accumulates lessons rather than being rewritten wholesale. In the figure below, red arrows mark the promoted lineage from candidate 0 to the best candidate (11), with scores in parentheses.
  • System-Aware Merge takes two qualifying descendants of a common ancestor and assembles a child module-by-module. For each module, if one descendant changed the ancestor’s prompt and the other left it untouched, the child inherits the changed version; if both descendants changed it, the child inherits from the higher-scoring parent (ties broken randomly); if neither changed it, it stays at the ancestor’s version. No LLM call is made — the whole step is a textual combine over existing prompts, which is why the paper calls it system-aware crossover rather than a mutation. Merge works only when the two parents have explored disjoint modules, so complementary improvements can compose without stepping on each other.

Parent selection is Pareto-based rather than greedy. Instead of always mutating the best-scoring candidate, GEPA maintains a per-task score matrix over its history and samples parents from the Pareto frontier — the set of candidates that no other candidate beats on every task — which prevents a locally strong candidate from dominating the search. The paper reports two named variants, “GEPA” using reflective mutation only and “GEPA+Merge” using both mutation and merge; both share the Pareto-based selector and the minibatch-then-full-set gate. The optimizer is agnostic to the downstream task: it needs a trajectory sampler, a metric, and a reflector LM.

Results

Six tasks — HotpotQA [4], HoVer [5], IFBench [6], PUPA [3], AIME-2025 [7], and LiveBench-Math [8] — using GPT-4.1 Mini and Qwen3-8B as task models.

  • Qwen3-8B: GEPA beats GRPO on five of the six benchmarks, losing only on AIME-2025. IFBench makes the gap sharp — GEPA reaches 38.61% after 678 rollouts, above GRPO’s 35.88% at 24,000. Averaged across the six tasks, GEPA is +6% over GRPO and up to +20% on the best task, with up to fewer rollouts (trajectories sampled from the current policy during training). GEPA+Merge is less reliable here: it also trails GRPO on IFBench and PUPA, which the paper attributes to Merge’s hyperparameters being tuned for GPT-4.1 Mini rather than Qwen3-8B.
  • GPT-4.1 Mini: GEPA is evaluated as a drop-in prompt optimizer against MIPROv2 [9] in two settings (instruction-only “MIPROv2-No-Demos” and joint instruction-plus-few-shot “MIPROv2”), Trace [10] with its OptoPrime optimizer, and TextGrad [11] . GEPA wins on every benchmark, with margins as wide as 11% (HotpotQA, PUPA). The abstract highlights +12% on AIME-2025. A GEPA-Qwen-Opt variant optimized entirely on Qwen3-8B gets +9% when run on GPT-4.1 Mini without modification, outperforming every baseline that was optimized directly on GPT-4.1 Mini.

Beyond benchmarks, the paper reports GEPA as a promising inference-time search strategy for CUDA kernel optimization, iteratively improving kernels against a PyTorch-eager baseline.

My Notes

  • Reflection beats policy gradients: GRPO wastes signal already present in each trajectory, in three ways.
    • Information content: GRPO consumes a trajectory as a single scalar reward (normalized against the group’s own mean and standard deviation, the “Group Relative” that replaces PPO’s learned critic), throwing away which tool call was wrong, which instruction was ambiguous, which demonstration misled the model. A reflector LM reading the same trajectory can name all three and edit the one prompt that caused the failure.
    • Variance: because each rollout contributes one noisy scalar, GRPO needs thousands of rollouts before the gradient estimate stabilizes. A natural-language critique encodes structured per-module diagnosis, so one rollout already yields usable signal.
    • Credit assignment: GRPO’s policy-gradient update spreads the scalar reward across every token of every module in the rollout, even when only one module was responsible. Reflection attributes the failure to a single module and leaves the rest alone.
    • The same pattern shows up in Self-Refine and Reflexion, where verbal feedback outperforms scalar reward at comparable compute. GEPA is the first paper I have seen that posts the head-to-head against GRPO on matched tasks.
  • The Pareto-frontier selector is the generalizable part: Sampling mutation parents from the Pareto frontier rather than argmax prevents collapse to a single best candidate, which is the same mode-collapse problem that shows up in evolutionary prompt search and RL fine-tuning. The mechanism is general enough to drop into any iterative search where candidates have multi-dimensional scores (accuracy vs. cost, or task A vs. task B), and I expect to see it reused well past prompt optimization.
  • Beating MIPROv2 without Bayesian optimization: This is a substantive methodological claim. MIPROv2 [9] spends its budget on a Bayesian surrogate over instruction and demonstration hyperparameters. GEPA discards the surrogate and spends the same budget on reflective rewrites plus merge. The result suggests the Bayesian model in MIPROv2 was under-using the trajectory information MIPROv2 already had access to, and the proposer was not reading the failures carefully enough. Several authors overlap between the two papers, so the comparison is a within-lab course-correction rather than an external critique.
  • The paper doesn’t say what reflector it used: Appendix E.2 lists Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1 Mini as the task models but never specifies the reflection LM. The gepa-ai/gepa repo quickstart pairs GPT-5 as reflector with GPT-4.1 Mini as task, a stronger model reading a weaker one’s trajectories. Without the reflector spec or an ablation, we can’t tell whether GEPA corroborates or contradicts the just-ask calibration [12] and uncertainty-quantification findings that single-model self-evaluation is unreliable.

item.title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Vasco Schiavo, writing on the Inference Notes Substack, derives why agent token costs explode and fits the predicted curves against real benchmark traces. The core claim: each turn re-sends the entire conversation history, so total input tokens pile up as a triangular number , quadratic in turns, while output tokens grow linearly.

The growth law

Prompt caching does not change the shape of this picture, but it changes which cells are cheap. Green cells below are cached input, billed at a fraction of the fresh rate (typically around 10%). The triangle still grows quadratically, but the dominant term becomes cheap re-reads instead of full-price input, so over the practical turn range the total cost looks linear even though the underlying formula is not.

The full with-cache cost formula is , still quadratic in with the term just multiplied by the small constant . The post argues that once caching is deployed, the linear term dominates over the practical turn range, so it fits the cached data with a line rather than a quadratic. The takeaway it pulls out: without caching, cost scales as ; with caching, cost scales as plus a negligible correction.

Fits on SWE-bench

To test those predictions on real data, the post fits two curve shapes — for no-cache and for with-cache — against cumulative paid tokens per turn on SWE-bench traces from the OpenHands evaluation index, across three models: GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Flash, and Claude Opus 4.6. Each coefficient has a concrete interpretation:

  • — per-turn verbosity. How many fresh tokens each turn contributes on average. A large means the model (or its harness) is pushing a lot of new content per turn.
  • — cache-era marginal cost. The effective per-turn cost once caching is doing its job. A small means cache hits are carrying most of the load. A large means the cache is not catching much.

In all three panels below, red is the no-cache median (dashed line = quadratic fit), blue is the with-cache median (dashed line = linear fit), and the pink band is the interquartile range (IQR) across task instances.

The three fits split along both axes:

Model (per-turn verbosity) ≈ fresh tokens/turn (cache-era marginal cost) Trajectory length
GPT-5.2 0.00050 1,000 0.0095 ~75
Gemini-3-Flash 0.00015 300 0.0086 ~175
Claude Opus 4.6 0.00046 920 0.0008 ~80

GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.6 are roughly matched on (around 1,000 fresh tokens per turn), while Gemini-3-Flash is a third of that, reflecting shorter responses and more compact tool calls. On , the three separate sharply: Opus’s is more than 10× shallower than the other two, meaning a higher cache hit rate, less fresh content per turn, or both at Anthropic’s end. That is why, on the Opus panel above, the with-cache line almost disappears into the x-axis against a no-cache peak of 3.7M tokens.

My Notes

  • Tension with “Where Claude Code tokens go”. Reading this alongside Where Claude Code tokens go surfaces a tension. Mnimiy’s proxy measured ~13% of Claude Code cost going to conversation-history re-reads and another ~10% to cache misses on session resume, together about a quarter of spend on the re-read triangle. But the SWE-bench Opus 4.6 fit here puts with-cache marginal cost at , so flat that re-reads should barely register. The gap is probably the cache-hit-rate assumption: SWE-bench traces one continuous session under near-ideal cache conditions, while real Claude Code usage invalidates the cache constantly — 5-minute timeouts on coffee breaks, CLAUDE.md edits, hook changes, tool reordering — pushing re-reads back to full price and moving the user onto the steeper no-cache curve.

  • IQR variance across the three models. Fitting to the median across ~500 tasks smooths away the tail that actually burns money, and the post barely addresses how wide that tail is. The no-cache interquartile bands differ sharply. Opus at has a band about 0.8M wide on a 3.7M median — roughly 20% of the median width. Gemini at is in a different regime: the median is 8M tokens and the upper quartile reaches 16M, so just the upper half of the IQR equals the median itself. GPT-5.2 sits in between. Some of that is Gemini running longer trajectories, which lets cumulative variance compound. But even at similar turn counts the proportional spread is higher for Gemini, probably because its per-turn token count is more variable: tool calls ranging from small greps to full-file reads, or a subset of tasks dragging into verbose off-path exploration. With Q3 = 2× median, 25% of Gemini sessions cost at least double what the median fit would predict, before you hit true outliers. For anyone using these curves to forecast agent spend, a cumulative-token curve would be more decision-relevant than the median fit.

  • Gemini’s 2× trajectory length. Trajectory length itself differs markedly across models, and the post doesn’t explain why. Gemini-3-Flash runs out to ; GPT-5.2 tops out around and Opus 4.6 around . Even with Gemini’s leaner per-turn verbosity ( tokens/turn), the longer trajectories end up consuming more total tokens: cumulative no-cache at session end versus for Opus. If the tasks are roughly equivalent across runs, that is twice the work to reach comparable outcomes, which would look like a capability gap. But I can’t rule out harness-level differences: different per-model step limits, different tool-call styles (many small reads vs fewer large ones), or different early-exit thresholds could each produce the same pattern without implying anything about the model. Without OpenHands config detail it stays ambiguous. The observation worth holding onto either way: “leaner per turn” doesn’t translate to “cheaper overall” if it costs twice as many turns to finish.

  • The two-line fix anecdote. The author notes in passing that the OpenAI cache slope looked several times steeper than theory predicted, traced it to a bug in how their own code was calling OpenAI’s cache API, and shaved the slope down with a two-line fix. That is a useful case for regression-testing cache behavior against a theoretical baseline. Any provider whose cached slope deviates from by more than some margin is either misconfigured in your client or mis-documented upstream.

  • Prompt-prefix stability, not just size. Prompt-prefix stability is what actually decides whether caching works, and the best-practices list treats it as a small detail tucked inside the “keep system prompts clear, concise, and stable” bullet. Rotating system prompts, reordering tool definitions, or appending per-session memory to the front of the context all silently invalidate the cache: a single edit anywhere inside the cached prefix flips the whole thing back to full price. That deserves its own bullet near the top of the list, not a clause inside one about size. The closest comparable analysis at another layer is Reiner Pope’s blackboard derivation of frontier LLM economics, which does the same thing one level down at the hardware layer: derive from the formula, calibrate to public prices.

  • Claude Opus 4.7’s New Tokenizer: ~40% More Tokens Than 4.6: the token-count input to this cost model, where a tokenizer change shifts every term in the quadratic.
  • Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries: attacks the same growing-context cost from the model side, compressing the cache the triangular re-read formula re-bills.
  • Agentic Coding Is a Trap: the long-trajectory agent workflows whose turn counts () drive the quadratic cost analyzed here.
